‘Shrinking space for diplomacy raising risks in South Asia’. • Former SPD chief says nuclear-armed states have no space for war • Growing reliance on hard power, emerging technologies creating new challenges • Senator Mushahid insists Pakistan emerging as ‘credible middle power’ ISLAMABAD: Adviser to the National Command Authority and former director general of the Strategic Plans Division (SPD) Lt Gen (retd) Mazhar Jamil has warned that the erosion of traditional arms-control frameworks, shrinking space for diplomacy and growing reliance on hard power and emerging technologies are creating new challenges to strategic stability in South Asia. Speaking at the seventh edition of the “Training of the Trainers” workshop on strategic matters organised by the Centre for International Strategic Studies (CISS), Islamabad, Gen Jamil said the global and regional strategic environment was becoming increasingly complex. He said persistent threat perceptions, unresolved disputes such as Kashmir and India’s military posturing had contributed to continuing security tensions in the region. “Strategic stability cannot be separated from the underlying political realities,” he said, cautioning that Indian military adventurism and hegemonic approaches in a nuclearised South Asia carried unacceptable risks. Referring to the experience of May 2025, Gen Jamil stressed that there was no space for war between two nuclear-armed states. He also highlighted Pakistan’s nuclear deterrence, conventional capabilities, national resilience and cohesive response framework, including the principle of Quid Pro Quo Plus, saying these were aimed at ensuring that no aggressor could achieve its political or military objectives through force. Earlier, Maj Gen (retd) Syed Shahab Shahid, director general of Arms Control and Disarmament Affairs at the SPD, said the global arms-control, disarmament and non-proliferation architecture was facing growing challenges. He called for a balanced, equitable and non-discriminatory approach that took into account the legitimate security concerns of all states. Gen Shahid said the continued modernisation and diversification of nuclear and strategic capabilities, alongside emerging developments in South Asia, were reshaping the strategic environment and creating new challenges to strategic stability. He warned that the selective application of non-proliferation norms and security arrangements could undermine confidence in the existing international security architecture. He stressed the need for a consistent and inclusive approach to strengthening strategic stability, reducing risks and advancing meaningful arms-control and non-proliferation objectives. The officials also pointed to disruptive technologies and growing reliance on hard power as factors complicating efforts to reduce risks and prevent conflict in the region. The workshop brought together senior professors and academics from universities across Pakistan, along with think-tank professionals, foreign policy experts and diplomats. It aimed to strengthen understanding of contemporary strategic issues and develop the capacity of academics and trainers to contribute to informed discourse on strategic stability, nuclear deterrence, arms control and non-proliferation. In his opening remarks, CISS Executive Director Amb Ali Sarwar Naqvi reflected on Pakistan’s strategic environment, tracing the evolution of its regional relevance and the opportunities and challenges shaping its security landscape. He highlighted Pakistan’s role as a diplomatic actor and its stated commitment to regional stability, while underscoring the importance of effective strategic responses to an increasingly complex security environment. In his keynote address, Senator Mushahid Hussain Sayed said Pakistan was emerging as a credible middle power in the evolving international order. He said Pakistan’s ability to mediate, engage and build partnerships in an increasingly fragmented world reflected the country’s “growing strategic weight”. Published in Dawn, September 19th, 2026

Dialogue needed. AS the situation in Yemen remains explosive, with the potential to spark a wider military conflagration in the region, as well as global economic chaos, Pakistan has taken a balanced position on the Saudi-Houthi conflict. While reaffirming support for Saudi Arabia on Thursday, and terming the situation around Bab al-Mandeb “exceptionally serious”, the Foreign Office said that “dialogue and diplomacy” were required, not “coercive measures”. This should answer questions pertaining to Pakistan’s commitments regarding its defence pacts with the kingdom . Though Islamabad remains committed to Riyadh’s security, at this time it supports a negotiated settlement to the conflict with the pro-Iran Houthis. It is a logical position for Pakistan to take, for while Saudi Arabia’s security is important, it would be unwise to jump into an open-ended quagmire. The region’s recent history supports this position. Saudi Arabia and the UAE — with Western military support — had been unable to dislodge the Houthis since the Saudi military campaign began in 2015, and in 2022, Riyadh opted for a ceasefire, which has now collapsed. To simply dub the Houthis Iranian ‘proxies’ is simplistic. While the Zaidi Shia movement has strong ties to Iran, it is an indigenous Yemeni group with centuries-old cultural and political roots in their homeland, and the support of local tribes, particularly in the north. Therefore, it cannot be bombed into oblivion. Any solution to the Yemeni imbroglio must involve the Houthis. The humanitarian situation in Yemen itself is dire. Nearly 100,000 people have been uprooted in the latest round of fighting, while the UN says that around 20m people require aid as they have to contend with “acute hunger”. Yemen’s health system has also collapsed due to the never-ending war. Externally, the closure of Bab al-Mandeb by the Houthis could deliver a painful blow to an already frail global economy. And if the conflict draws in other regional states, the situation could transform into a dangerous maelstrom. Hence, any call for dialogue makes sense. There are reports that the Saudis have sought talks with the Houthis via Oman. Hopefully, this channel can deliver positive results and lead to a halt in fighting. For long-term peace, the Houthis must pledge to keep Bab al-Mandeb open for all, and stop their attacks on Saudi Arabia. In return, the kingdom must lift its blockade of Houthi-held territory. Once calm is established, talks can begin for a broad-based Yemeni government, which incorporates all the country’s tribal and confessional stakeholders. Ultimately, any peace agreement must guarantee the security of both Yemen and Saudi Arabia, and lead to an inclusive system where all Yemeni parties are accommodated. The forgotten NSP. WHEN the PTI government introduced Pakis­tan’s first-ever National Security Policy (NSP) in 2022, the framework placed its primary emphasis on geo-economics and the pursuit of economic security. However, as this five-year policy nears expiration, it seems that the geo-economic vision and citizen-centric approach envisioned under the NSP have failed to achieve their objectives. This lack of success stems from three major reasons. The foremost reason is the curse of political discontinuity. When prime minister Imran Khan unveiled Pakistan’s first-ever NSP in January 2022, it was hailed as a revolutionary pivot towards a citizen-centric geo-economic future. Yet, just months later, the predictable wheel of Pakistani political instability turned, and with the ouster of the PTI government , the strategic document was promptly relegated to bureaucratic limbo. It seems that in Pakistan’s deeply polarised political landscape, structural continuity is a luxury. Successive administrations traditionally suffer from a profound ‘ownership gap’, and view the policy blueprints of their predecessors with suspicion. This does not mean that the incoming coalition government ripped up the NSP. Rather, the subsequent administrations of the PDM alliance and then the PML-N-led coalition found itself completely consumed by the base instincts of political survival and immediate fiscal fires. These priorities diluted institutional focus and shifted the national priority from long-term economic integration to immediate to short-term emergency bailouts. Secondly, a viable geo-economic vision cannot survive in a fortress state. Rather, it demands liberalised trade policies, open borders, and a hyper-competitive export sector. But Islamabad remains wedded to an inward-looking protective regime, that maintains high tariffs on intermediate inputs averaging eight per cent, which is twice as high as Indian and Bangladeshi standards, effectively cutting off Pakistan’s industries from global value chains. This protectionism has pushed Pakistan’s export capacity against a hard structural ceiling, rendering regional competitive advantage remarkably weak. When the NSP was introduced, Pakistan’s total exports had reached a record $39.52 billion. Yet, while the policy promised a geo-economic turnaround to boost these numbers, subsequent years brought severe political instability and soaring energy tariffs that caused total exports to contract. Third, for Pakistan, a fractured and hostile neighbourhood is a major constraint in realising its geo-economic strategy. Even the most robust economic policies are ultimately at the mercy of geography. The regional assumptions that underpinned Pakistan’s first-ever NSP collapsed almost as soon as the ink dried. At the time of the NSP’s release, there was cautious optimism in the strategic community of Islamabad. Backchannel diplomacy with India had successfully culminated in a 2021 understanding to ‘strictly observe’ a ceasefire along the Line of Control. This development indicated a slow path towards normalisation despite the scar of the 2019 Pulwama-Balakot crisis. However, New Delhi’s uncompromising policy of refusing any structural dialogue effectively froze the eastern front for Pakistan. Furthermore, New Delhi’s subsequent decision to hold the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance , coupled with the intense four-day armed hostilities of May 2025 , has effectively slammed the door on any lingering hopes for normalisation in the foreseeable future. A viable geo-economic vision cannot survive in a fortress state. Simultaneously, Islamabad’s grand calculations on its western border have turned to dust. The initial hope that the Afghan Taliban regime in Kabul would secure transit corridors to Central Asia was quickly shattered. Instead of acting as a cooperative partner, Kabul chose to prioritise its ideological fraternity with the TTP over its relationship with Islamabad. This policy decision of the Taliban regime plunged the Pak-Afghan border into a volatile cycle of skirmishes, trade closures, and a sev­ere domestic security crisis that completely derai­led the NSP’s transit-hub ambitions. Resultantly, bilateral commerce between Pakistan and Afghanistan, Afghan transit trade volume via Pakistan, and third-country exports through Pakistan contracted sharply. Adding to this paralysis, Pakistan’s southwestern frontier remains structurally locked. While the diplomatic relationship with Iran has managed to be stable and progressive, the pervasive American sanctions regime has severely strangled any realistic potential to further enhance economic ties with Tehran. Pakistan’s geo-economic vision cannot be realised until Islamabad radically restructures its domestic priorities and foreign policy architecture on three major fronts. First and foremost, Islamabad must insulate its core economic strategy from the volatile swings of its political cycles. This demands a rare moment of political maturity, where cross-party consensus elevates econo­mic diplomacy to a non-partisan national objecti­­ve and ensures that a change at the Prime Minister’s Office doesn’t translate into abandonment of the country’s long-term economic roadmap. Second, Islamabad must formally divorce its economy from its security apparatus, and treat them as separate, independent domains so that trade channels are never again sacrificed to the knee-jerk impulses of geopolitical friction. Instead of attempting a grand, macro-level regional integration that is easily checked by state-level hostility, Islamabad must pivot towards a bottom-up approach that maximises its leverage by creating dedicated border economic zones and automated, high-tech transit terminals with its eastern and western neighbours. Third, to transition from a security state to a true citizen-centric development state, Pakistan must boldly address its structural bottlenecks. This means dismantling the protectionist tariff walls that stifle innovation, aggressively diversifying the low-tech export basket beyond textiles, and creating a stable, predictable regulatory environment capable of attracting genuine foreign direct investment. Regionally, while the geopolitical landscape remains treacherous, Islamabad cannot afford to be economically isolated. It must leverage its strategic partnership with Beijing to optimise the next phase of CPEC, while simultaneously utilising creative, localised trade arrangements with Kabul and Delhi, where formal diplomatic breakthroughs remain stalled. Islamabad must realise that, while it has regained significant strategic importance in the Middle East, and beyond to some extent, it finds itself increasingly isolated within its own region. To fix this, Pakistan must fundamentally rethink its regional and domestic policies so it can truly benefit from its renewed global influence and turn its geo-economic objectives into lasting economic growth. The writer is a strategic analyst of international security. The views expressed are his own. X: @itskhurramabbas Published in Dawn, September 19th, 2026

Sindh’s first Gender Parity Report highlights challenges amid gains. • Overall female literacy stands at 47pc, only 27.52pc for rural women • Over 4.08m girls between five and 16 remain out of school • Only 4.34pc in police force, 13.7pc in judiciary • Maternal mortality falls to 224 per 100,000 births • Number of women contesting general elections rises from 23 in 2018 to 53 in 2024 KARACHI: The Sindh government on Friday unveiled its first-ever Gender Parity Report, a landmark assessment of gender equality across the province. While highlighting notable gains in maternal health, female employment and political participation, the report identifies persistent gender gaps in literacy, school enrolment, workforce representation, digital access and decision-making roles. The report, presented to the Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah by Special Assistant to CM (SACM) on Human Rights Rajvir Singh Sodho here at the CM House, provides the first comprehensive provincial baseline on gender disparities and progress across key sectors, including health, education, justice, governance, economic participation and demographics, said a press release issued by the CM House. According to the report, Sindh’s population reached 55.69 million in 2023, growing at an annual rate of 2.57 per cent, with a sex ratio of 108.76 males for every 100 females. The report records steady progress in the health sector, where public allocations increased from Rs214.5 billion in 2023-24 to Rs267.54bn in 2024-25 and are projected to rise further to Rs318.22bn in 2025-26. Maternal mortality declined significantly from 314 to 224 deaths per 100,000 live births, while neonatal mortality stood at 24 deaths per 1,000 live births. Despite these gains, education sector remains one of the province’s most significant challenges. The report shows male literacy at 68 per cent compared to 47pc among females, while literacy among rural women remains critically low at 27.52pc. More than 4.08m girls between the ages of five and 16 remain out of school, underscoring the need for urgent and sustained action. In the justice sector, women continue to be underrepresented, accounting for only 4.34pc of the police force, 18.3pc of prosecutors and 13.7pc of judges. The report also documented 3,085 reported cases of gender-based violence during 2024, highlighting the need for stronger protection mechanisms and improved access to justice. The report also highlights encouraging trends in governance, political participation and economic inclusion. Women’s voter registration exceeded 12m, while the number of women contesting general elections increased from 23 in 2018 to 53 in 2024. While female employment increased from 2.48m to 3.32m, the report notes that barriers related to digital connectivity, financial inclusion, skills development, entrepreneurship and access to decent work continue to limit women’s full economic participation. The report concludes that while Sindh has achieved measurable progress in several sectors, sustained reforms, stronger institutions, improved district-level data systems and focused investments will be essential to achieving inclusive, equitable and gender-responsive development throughout the province. Murad calls for targeted reforms The CM directed all provincial departments to undertake targeted reforms, strengthen gender-responsive governance and improve access to education, healthcare, economic opportunities and representation for women and girls. He described the report as a critical policy tool that would guide evidence-based planning, resource allocation and institutional reforms aimed at advancing gender equality across Sindh. “Gender equality is not only a matter of social justice but also a prerequisite for sustainable development,” Mr Shah said. “The report gives us a clear understanding of where progress has been achieved and where urgent interventions are required. We will use these findings to strengthen policies and programmes that empower women and girls across the province.” Reaffirming the Pakistan Peoples Party’s long-standing commitment to women’s empowerment, Mr Shah paid tribute to former prime minister Benazir Bhutto, describing her as a global symbol of courage, democratic values and gender equality. “Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto dedicated her political struggle to the empowerment of women, the protection of fundamental rights and the creation of equal opportunities for all citizens. Her vision continues to guide our efforts to build a more inclusive and equitable Sindh,” he said. The CM instructed departments to strengthen gender-disaggregated data systems, improve monitoring mechanisms, enhance coordination among institutions and ensure that women’s needs and perspectives are integrated into planning and budgeting processes. He said the Sindh government remained committed to removing these barriers through targeted investments, institutional reforms and gender-responsive development planning. “Our goal is to create a Sindh where every woman and girl has equal opportunities to learn, work, lead and contribute to society. The findings of this report will help us accelerate that journey and ensure that no one is left behind,” he said. Presenting the report, Mr Sodho described it as a milestone achievement for Sindh’s human rights framework and a foundation for gender-responsive policymaking. “This is the first comprehensive provincial assessment that consolidates gender-related indicators from multiple sectors into a single analytical framework. It provides policymakers with reliable evidence to identify gaps, track progress and formulate targeted interventions,” he said. Published in Dawn, September 19th, 2026

Trump says Denmark to give US 'permanent control' over Greenland security. US President Donald Trump said on Friday that he had struck a deal with Denmark to give Washington “permanent control” over Greenland’s security that would bar Russia and China from setting up bases in the Arctic territory. Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has repeatedly insisted that Washington needed to control Greenland for strategic reasons, alarming Nato ally Denmark and sparking fierce pushback from the alliance. Denmark and Greenland — an autonomous territory controlled by Copenhagen — both hailed the deal and said they would sign it on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York next week. But the terms of the deal remain uncertain, and Denmark maintains its sovereignty remains intact. In a statement, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen described the deal as “an agreement which at the same time recognises the sovereignty an territorial integrity of the kingdom and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination”. “I am pleased to announce that the United States of America has entered into an Agreement with The Kingdom of Denmark, and Greenland, that gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland,” Trump said on his Truth Social network. “From now on, no US adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval.” The 80-year-old said it was an “‘Infinite Life’ Agreement, there is no end!” and said Washington would immediately start building up a large military presence in the territory. ‘Good agreement’ Trump has repeatedly warned about Russia and China trying to establish a foothold in Greenland as a strategic battle for supremacy in a warming Arctic unfolds, and the State Department left no doubt that they would not be allowed to do so. “This agreement guarantees that China and Russia cannot have a base in Greenland, they cannot send troops to Greenland, and the necessary mechanisms are in place to prevent investment in sensitive sectors,” a State Department official said. At the Davos economic forum this past January, Trump reached a purported deal with Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte over the future of Greenland, the terms of which have remained vague. Frederiksen had said on Monday that she was “optimistic” that ongoing discussions with the United States and Greenland since January could resolve the dispute. She said on Friday she was “pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement for Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark and the United States,” adding that it was “good for Nato and Europe.” Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said the deal with the United States “strengthens” the territory’s security. Nato tensions Trump gave no details about how the deal would work, and it was not clear if it was linked to or substantially different from the Rutte deal. But several media outlets have reported that the United States wants to open three new military bases in southern Greenland, in addition to the Pituffik base it already has in the north of the territory. A 1951 defence pact, updated in 2004, already allows Washington to ramp up troop deployments and military installations on the island provided it informs Denmark and Greenland in advance. At the height of the crisis, Trump would not rule out using force to seize the territory of 57,000 inhabitants, sowing anxiety within the EU and Nato. Since then, tensions have cooled somewhat, and in an apparent move to assuage Trump, Nato launched a new mission to bolster security in the Arctic.

Gemini hacked 3 companies in first known breakout by Google's AI. Google’s Gemini model accessed the internet and hacked other companies during a test of its cybersecurity capabilities, the first known example of the company’s AI systems autonomously committing such an act. The hacks occurred in May during a cybersecurity test conducted by Irregular, an independent company that conducts cybersecurity evaluations. During a standard testing evaluation, Gemini found public information online and guessed credentials to access three websites it thought were within the scope of its test, Heather Adkins, Google’s vice president of security engineering, said in a statement. “We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they’ve now made to their testing processes,” Adkins said. “These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly.” An Irregular spokesperson said the incident involved the same issue that affected other AI labs and that all relevant labs were notified in late July. “All known issues on our end were remedied and resolved weeks ago,” the spokesperson said. Similar incidents linked to Irregular were disclosed by Meta, Anthropic and OpenAI . Meta said in August the incident did not involve a sandbox escape or sophisticated cyberattack, while Irregular said it was working on best practices for securely conducting AI cybersecurity evaluations. The incidents have raised questions about the safeguards needed as AI agents gain greater autonomy and access to the internet and computer systems. In one of the cases, the Gemini model guessed passwords until it gained access to a protected system. In the other two cases, the model found credentials in a public repository that allowed it to then access protected systems, according to the Wall Street Journal . Adkins said that in all three instances, the model ceased its hacking.

Trump extends push for $100,000 H-1B visa fee by another year. President Donald Trump has extended an executive order that would impose a fee of $100,000 for H-1B non-immigrant visas by another year, the White House said on Friday. US employers seeking to hire skilled foreign workers can use the federal government’s H-1B visa programme for a fee, allowing tech and other professionals from abroad to work in the United States for a few years. Trump, who has pursued an aggressive immigration crackdown, has criticised the programme and wants to permanently raise the fee from between $2,000 and $5,000 to at least $100,000, though the attempt has faced legal challenges. A Boston-based appeals court is reviewing a June decision by a federal judge who deemed the higher fee imposed by the Trump administration illegal and blocked the government from collecting it. Another court is considering whether a judge properly rejected a challenge to the fee by the US Chamber of Commerce, the largest US business lobbying group. Trump’s initial order for a fee hike, first released in September 2025, was set to expire this month. It did not apply to visas granted to foreign citizens already in the United States on student visas, who make up a large share of new H-1B recipients, or to renewals of current visas. Despite criticism that some companies use the visas to hire lower-paid foreign workers instead of Americans, business groups and companies say they help recruit highly skilled professionals and address a lack of qualified US workers in some industries. The visas, established by Congress in 1990, are especially critical for tech companies seeking to recruit from India and China. Changes to how potential visa holders are scrutinised and processed have impacted companies’ hiring and expansion plans, with some top H-1B users, such as Google parent company Alphabet, moving to increase operations in India.

On Our Radar eschelhaas Fri, 09/11/2026 - 00:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Special Coverage / Global 11 September 2026 20+ minutes On Our Radar On Our Radar scans conflicts and crises around the globe every week and features some of the hotspots Crisis Group’s analysts are closely watching. Whether an under-reported trend or a headline-grabbing development, our field experts explain why it matters or what should be done. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print 11 September 2026 IRAN The International Atomic Energy Agency referred Iran to the UN Security Council Wednesday for breaching its nuclear non-proliferation obligations, marking the first time in twenty years the organisation has taken such a step. Tehran condemned the decision, blaming U.S. and Israeli strikes on its nuclear facilities for disrupting the agency’s inspections. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says concerns about Iran’s lacklustre cooperation with the UN watchdog have been mounting for years, capped by over a year of blocked access to key sites bombed by the U.S. and Israel in June 2025. Given that UN sanctions were already reinstated last year, and the expectation that China and Russia will shield it from additional punitive measures at the Security Council, the referral may harden Iran’s obduracy rather than cajole it into overdue cooperation. LEBANON Israel stepped up its attacks in southern Lebanon over the weekend with strikes that killed nearly 30 people and wounded dozens more. While Israel claimed that it had targeted Hizbollah arms caches and military installations, the assaults killed several children and medical staff. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Israel’s lethal escalation could continue, unless it faces strong pressure from the U.S., its most important ally, to desist. Washington sponsored a Lebanon-Israel ceasefire struck in late June but, over two months later, the deal remains largely unfulfilled, with Israeli military action continuing and Hizbollah refusing to disarm. SOMALIA Somali piracy has seen an uptick this year, with at least six hijackings of cargo ships and smaller vessels since April. The turmoil resulting from the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has created opportune conditions for pirates, with fewer naval patrols off the Somali coast and more commercial traffic in nearby waters as ships are diverted from the Bab al-Mandab and the Strait of Hormuz. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says the number of pirate attacks is far below what it was during the heyday of Red Sea piracy fifteen years ago. The current trajectory is concerning, however, and more raids are bound to occur, absent international and local measures both offshore and on land to combat the phenomenon. 4 September 2026 HAITI Armed gang members stormed the commune of Kenscoff, overlooking Port-au-Prince, overnight on 23-24 August, killing at least 47 people and abducting more than 50, whom they threatened to kill if security forces go after the gang in that area. At least thirteen abductees have subsequently been released. Briefing the UN Security Council on 28 August, UN envoy Carlos Ruiz Massieu said the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) would beef up its presence in the capital, while Haitian units would send reinforcements to Kenscoff. He also urged the GSF, which remains far short of its planned 5,500-person strength, to deploy in full without delay. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the Kenscoff massacre is the latest indication that gangs are on the offensive as the GSF assembles. U.S. - IRAN After a month-long lull, the U.S. resumed attacks on Iranian soil over the weekend, first striking rocket launchers on Larak island that Washington said were preparing to deploy sea mines, then hitting dozens of military targets along Iran’s southern coast. Tehran responded with missile and drone fire at bases hosting U.S. forces in the Gulf. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick comes as the Trump administration tries to isolate Tehran financially through increased sanctions and a naval blockade, while in parallel undermining Iranian efforts to control the Strait of Hormuz by escorting vessels through the waterway. While Washington's approach is to squeeze wherever possible and strike whenever it deems necessary – for example, in response to Iranian strikes or efforts to rebuild its military capabilities – the Islamic Republic could counter with additional strikes of its own on U.S. assets and allies, along with further attacks on shipping. THAILAND Overnight on 22 August, militants in Thailand’s three southernmost provinces staged over 50 attacks in four hours, including bombings and arson attempts at local administrative offices, shops and other buildings. Three passersby were injured. Further incidents followed on 23 and 29 August despite tightened security. Authorities blamed Barisan Revolusi Nasional Patani Melayu (Patani-Malay National Revolutionary Front, BRN), which has fought Bangkok’s rule since 2004. Such coordinated attacks are routine, says Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler, but the scale of this campaign was unusual. It was likely intended to discredit the state, demonstrate insurgents’ reach and heighten pressure on the government to resume peace talks that have occurred intermittently since 2013. Thailand’s chief negotiator has reportedly proposed bringing technical-level talks with BRN forward from October to this month, in part to determine the reasons for the attacks. 21 August 2026 CHINA - SOUTH KOREA Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi paid a two-day visit to South Korea this week to discuss bilateral ties, Korean peninsula tensions and broader Asian affairs. The trip came three days after U.S. President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea. Trump also said he is willing to meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, as he did during his first term. These two unilateral announcements in turn prompted South Korean President Lee Jae-myung to reiterate his call for Seoul to bolster its own defences, for instance by acquiring nuclear-powered submarines and regaining independent control of its military in the event of hostilities. (Its forces would now be under U.S. command in a wartime contingency.) Crisis Group expert William Yang says the U.S.-South Korean friction has given Beijing an opening to deepen its own engagement with Seoul. It may now seek to present itself as the main mediator on the Korean peninsula, given its links with Pyongyang. The annexation drive also undermines the Trump administration’s twenty-point plan for Gaza. 6 February 2026 GAZA Israel carried out strikes across the Gaza Strip Wednesday, killing at least 24 Palestinians. The Israeli army claimed it was targeting a Hamas commander and responding to fire upon its troops, but civilians accounted for most of the casualties. The death toll among Palestinians in Gaza since the October 2025 ceasefire has now topped 550. Humanitarian needs also remain acute amid aid shortfalls; the Rafah crossing with Egypt has opened, after a long wait, but deliveries are still tightly restricted. Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein says the latest violence underscores how tenuous the ceasefire remains despite formally entering its second phase, when the sides are supposed to begin addressing issues of long-term security, governance and reconstruction. Diplomats need to press Israel to release its chokehold on Gaza and push for continued progress on the truce’s terms. PAKISTAN Police backed by soldiers reportedly killed more than 200 Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) fighters in raids throughout Balochistan, a south-western province next to Afghanistan, over the course of this week. The operations followed a rash of BLA attacks on police stations, military installations and residential areas that claimed 50 lives (33 civilians and 17 state personnel) over the weekend. Islamabad accuses the Afghan Taliban of harbouring the BLA high command, which they also say gets financial and logistical assistance from Pakistan’s arch-rival India. Crisis Group Executive Vice President Richard Atwood says the high death toll among the Baloch separatist insurgents shows that authorities planned the raids carefully, with a view to keeping civilians out of the crossfire. But these events are bound to increase tensions between Islamabad and Kabul, which are already high following clashes between Pakistani and Afghan Taliban forces last October, and to further chill relations between Islamabad and New Delhi. U.S. - COLOMBIA Presidents Donald Trump and Gustavo Petro met at the White House Tuesday after months of heated rhetoric prompted by disputes over issues such as migration, counter-narcotics cooperation and the 3 January U.S. raid grabbing Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Amid these exchanges, Trump went so far as to suggest that Colombia, too, might be a target of U.S. military action. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the meeting proved constructive, helping ease the tensions in the bilateral relationship and signalling that the two countries can continue working together to curb drug trafficking. The two presidents also discussed the tariff spat between Colombia and Ecuador, with Trump offering to mediate between these countries’ leaders. Resolving the immediate trade crisis could pave the way for stronger collaboration between Bogotá and Quito in fighting organised crime. 30 January 2026 COLOMBIA - ECUADOR The foreign ministers of Colombia and Ecuador met in Panama after a week in which a trade dispute escalated between the two countries. The standoff began last week, when Ecuador announced a 30 per cent tariff on Colombian imports, blaming Bogotá for insufficient action to stop drug trafficking along the shared border. Colombia retaliated with tariffs on Ecuadorian goods and a suspension of electricity exports. Ecuador then raised the fee for Colombian oil shipped through its pipelines tenfold from about $3 to $30 per barrel. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the meeting indicates that the two capitals understand the dispute will hurt both economies as well as weaken both states’ ability to confront security challenges on the frontier. Rather than acting in isolation, the two should mount a coordinated cross-border response, which is likely to be more effective in fighting transnational criminal networks. IRAN U.S. President Donald Trump told Iran Wednesday that it risks "major destruction" if it fails to negotiate a nuclear deal with Washington. The ultimatum follows earlier warnings of U.S. intervention over the Islamic Republic's repression of protests. The U.S. has dispatched additional naval assets, airpower and defensive systems to the Middle East. Tehran – along with some of its non-state allies in the region – has threatened retaliation if attacked. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says Iran is unlikely to meet the White House's sweeping demands, which encompass nuclear, missile and regional concessions, raising the likelihood of confrontation at a time when the Islamic Republic already faces increasing diplomatic isolation, mounting economic problems and outrage at its brutal crackdown on dissent. SOUTH SUDAN The South Sudanese army announced Sunday it is launching a major offensive to recapture territory in Jonglei state that has been seized by opposition forces and allied militias since hostilities intensified in December. The UN warned this week that mass troop mobilisation and inflammatory rhetoric from senior commanders have significantly heightened the risk of violence against civilians. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the escalation signals a clear slide toward full-scale war. The rapidly expanding conflict threatens to draw in neighbouring states, including Uganda, and to deepen South Sudan’s dangerous entanglement in the war in Sudan. 23 January 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO M23 rebels withdrew from Uvira, near the Burundian border, over last weekend, ending a tense month in which they controlled the South Kivu town. They had promised to pull out, likely due to U.S. pressure following a December summit in Washington between their main outside backer, the Rwandan president, and his Congolese counterpart. The Congolese army and allied Wazalendo militias re-entered Uvira this week, but in the interim chaos engulfed the town, with widespread looting and abuses against civilians, mainly by the Wazalendo. Of particular concern, says Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff, is the mounting ethnic tension in the area. The M23 insurgents, who portray themselves as defenders of the Tutsi people, took Uvira claiming that the Tutsi-related Banyamulenge living in town needed their protection. Primary responsibility for attacks on Banyamulenge residents lies with the Congolese authorities and their allies, but the rebels appear to have exposed these people to predictable retaliation after retreating. Another M23-aligned armed group, the Twiraneho, is involved in fighting around Uvira, also pointing to a pattern of inter-communal violence. GUATEMALA President Bernardo Arévalo declared a 30-day state of emergency Monday after inmates had taken more than 45 guards hostage at three prisons two days earlier. After the authorities regained control of one of the facilities, gang members outside jail killed ten policemen in retaliation. The state of emergency limits citizens' rights and gives state forces special powers such as making arrests without cause. It echoes the iron-fist approaches to public safety pursued by leaders in El Salvador and Ecuador. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says Arévalo, who won the 2024 election touting a progressive reform agenda but has since lost popularity, listened to demands from Guatemalans for a decisive response to an uptick in violent crime. If the measure delivers immediate results, it could help the president’s political standing. UGANDA Tensions simmered this week after the 15 January elections, which saw President Yoweri Museveni win another term with 71.65 per cent of the vote. The leading opposition candidate, Robert Kyagulanyi of the National Unity Party (NUP), rejected the result, alleging widespread fraud. He remains in hiding after dodging a police raid – staged for reasons that remain unclear – on his residence. The president's powerful son, army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba, said on social media Tuesday Kyagulanyi would be treated as an "outlaw/rebel" if he did not surrender within 48 hours. (He later deleted this and other inflammatory posts.) Meanwhile, authorities charged more than 100 NUP members with involvement in election day violence. An internet blackout has made details of the incidents difficult to verify. The official death toll is twelve, but both Kyagulanyi and Muhoozi have cited higher figures. The government says ten died when its forces were attacked at an opposition legislator's home, a version of events sharply contested by others who were present. Crisis Group expert Meron Elias says the opacity of events, along with Muhoozi’s threats, will likely keep the political temperature high following the polarising vote. 16 January 2026 CUBA The bodies of 32 Cuban soldiers killed during the 3 January U.S. raid in Venezuela arrived in Havana Thursday. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says Washington appears to be calculating that a deepening economic crisis in Cuba will mobilise the masses to bring about the regime’s collapse. The Cuban regime retains a strong military and solid ties to Russia and China, however, and previously has not hesitated to crush dissent. GREENLAND Several European NATO members have deployed troops to Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark, to beef up infrastructure and carry out joint military exercises after U.S. President Donald Trump repeatedly stated that the U.S. intends to acquire the island, by force if necessary. Wednesday’s meeting among the U.S., Greenland and Denmark in Washington failed to resolve “fundamental disagreement” on Greenland’s future, according to the Danish foreign minister. With Europe already buffeted by Russia's full-scale war in Ukraine, says Crisis Group expert Olga Oliker, this crisis will have dire implications for the future of NATO and European security writ large if the U.S. does not back down. SYRIA Thousands demonstrated in the north east Tuesday against government forces’ expulsion of Kurdish fighters from Aleppo. Since the last Kurdish fighters left the city Sunday, fighting shifted eastward, raising the risk of sustained confrontation. In early January, the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) clashed with the Syrian army in Aleppo as negotiations to integrate Syria’s north east under central government control stalled. Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says Damascus cannot take the whole region militarily, but it will likely keep applying pressure on the SDF. The U.S., which supports both sides, has kept a ceiling on escalation thus far and should use its leverage to bring the parties back to the negotiating table. 9 January 2026 CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC Provisional results show that President Faustin-Archange Touadéra has secured a third term after general elections on 28 December. The government has altered its subsidy policies but done little to dampen wider grievances. At least three dozen people have been killed as state forces crack down on protests that show little sign of slowing down. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says the Islamic Republic faces a major dilemma: it is neither willing nor able to adopt reforms that could meet expectations for political, social and economic change and on notice from U.S. President Donald Trump that outside intervention is possible if its repression intensifies. LEBANON Lebanon said it had passed a milestone in disarming Hizbollah, but the country’s fragile ceasefire deal with Israel remains imperilled. On Thursday, the Lebanese army announced that it had brought all weapons under state control in the southern area between the Litani River and the Israeli border. Israel immediately disputed the army’s assertion, saying Hizbollah retains military infrastructure in that region. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Beirut faces dangers ahead in any case. What Future for Venezuela after the U.S. Oil Carve-up? pzeiler Fri, 09/11/2026 - 11:11 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List US Energy Secretary Chris Wright (L) and Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodriguez (R) talk during a meeting over an oil agreement at the Miraflores Presidential Palace in Caracas on September 2, 2026. Juan Barreto / AFP Q&A / Latin America & Caribbean 11 September 2026 17 minutes What Future for Venezuela after the U.S. Oil Carve-up? The Trump administration has announced an agreement with Caracas that it says gives the U.S. a major stake in the Venezuelan oil industry. In this Q&A, Crisis Group experts Phil Gunson and Delaney Simon explore the reported deal’s ramifications. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Also available in Español Español English Related Tags Venezuela United States What happened? U.S. President Donald Trump announced on 28 August that his administration had reached an agreement that purportedly gives Washington control of 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven oil reserves, in what he called “the biggest oil deal in world history”. According to Trump, the 100-year concession – to be run by a private company under de facto U.S. government control – would more than double U.S. reserves, permit the U.S. to replenish its strategic stockpiles and alleviate pressure on fuel prices. The White House emphasised that the deal would come at no cost to the U.S. taxpayer. Venezuela’s government confirmed the arrangement, while offering conflicting details as to its duration and precise terms. The announcement is one more sign that the relationship between Caracas and Washington has mutated into one of diminished Venezuelan sovereignty and informal U.S. dominion, with a stress on extracting Venezuela’s natural resources. On 3 January, just hours after U.S. special forces captured President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores, whisking them to New York for trial on drug trafficking charges, Trump promised that the U.S. would “run” Venezuela and take “a tremendous amount of wealth out of the ground”. To replace Maduro, the U.S. endorsed former Vice President Delcy Rodríguez to be interim leader, making clear that her hold on the post would depend on staying in Trump’s good graces. [The U.S.] has brokered the greater part of [Venezuela’s] oil exports, channelling the proceeds into an account controlled by the U.S. Treasury. While the U.S. avoided the potentially disastrous fallout of dismantling the chavista regime in Caracas without a viable alternative, Washington has since swung to the other extreme of giving full backing to Rodríguez, in the process tightening its grip on Venezuela and its raw materials. It has brokered the greater part of the country’s oil exports, channelling the proceeds into an account controlled by the U.S. Treasury, which decides how and when the revenue is spent. In late January, weeks after Maduro was arraigned in a U.S. court, Venezuela’s interim government also passed a sweeping reform intended to draw foreign investors into the oil and gas industry by reducing tax and royalties due to the state, while allowing greater private participation in oil production. Despite the overhaul of the legal regime and the transformation of Venezuela-U.S. relations – which had been prickly under the late President Hugo Chávez (1999-2013) and downright hostile under Maduro’s authoritarian rule – the Trump administration has struggled to convince U.S. oil majors to invest more in Venezuela. Dilapidated infrastructure, including a crumbling electrical grid, will require years of costly repairs if new hydrocarbons operations in the country are to generate major profits. Investors are also concerned by the absence of rule of law and fear that any agreement reached with the de facto authorities could be reversed if they were to be overthrown or replaced by a democratically elected government. Frustrated by big oil’s reticence to dive into Venezuela, and under growing pressure ahead of U.S. midterm elections to lower gasoline prices as the Middle East war nudges them higher, the Trump administration has looked for alternative routes to boosting output. Both Rodríguez and Trump indicated that under the new agreement, seventeen oilfields would be developed, requiring an investment of $100 billion, and fattening the Venezuelan exchequer to the tune of more than $200 billion overall. Rodríguez, however, gave a markedly different account of some of the deal’s key terms. According to the Venezuelan leader, the agreement is to last for 25, not 100 years, and it does not involve relinquishing Venezuelan sovereign control of oil reserves. But the agreement’s text has not been made public; not even the Venezuelan parliament has seen it. Critics have therefore persisted in calling the deal an astonishing handover of strategic resources, one that may violate the Venezuelan constitution and that lacks clear guarantees of economic benefit for Venezuelans. What do we know about the deal’s contents? While the terms remain opaque, U.S. officials have said the arrangement gives Washington preferential purchasing rights and a 35 per cent stake in a private company that would operate the seventeen oilfields under a century-long lease. Roughly half these fields are in the Lake Maracaibo basin, the north-western area where the Venezuelan oil industry began over a century ago, but whose facilities are in a state of severe disrepair . The other half lie in the Orinoco Belt, just north of the Orinoco River in central Venezuela, where development would in some cases require building new roads, as well as housing, production facilities and pipelines. All the oilfields in Venezuela are state property. Washington would not control the fields directly, but would instead wield influence through a private company, North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), which now operates three of the seventeen fields and would hold the concessions to all of them . The U.S. State Department would have the right to purchase at production cost 20 per cent of the oil produced by all current and future fields run by NABEP. It would also have the right of “first refusal” on the remaining 80 per cent of production, giving the U.S. government the chance to buy oil ahead of any other customer. The Trump administration says it will have veto power in appointing the NABEP’s parent company’s board of directors, which appears not to exist yet. It also says a majority of members will have to be U.S. citizens. The U.S. government is no stranger to state-owned enterprises – it is involved in corporations that run everything from regional power grids (like the Tennessee Valley Authority) to rail (for example, Amtrak) and mail delivery (the U.S. Postal Service) – but such a level of control of another country’s natural resources, enabled by U.S. military action and secured through U.S. political influence, has not been common practice since Washington exercised quasi-colonial rule over various Latin American nations in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. In more recent history, the U.S. government has taken equity stakes in companies during crises – for example, to bail out the auto industry after the 2008 financial crisis. But, as a former Pentagon official told Crisis Group, there appears to be no comparable public interest reason to take a stake in NABEP. “They’re doing it because they can get away with it … and they are trying to take the oil”. The White House has named the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital to hold the equity stakes in NABEP, a move that conceals a complicated legal picture. The office, which was established in December 2022 under President Joe Biden to stimulate investment in technologies seen as critical to national security, is not currently authorised by Congress to take equity stakes in private companies. But its director, who performs another function as the senior advisor to the deputy secretary of defense , seems to have invoked the authority of the Pentagon’s Office of Industrial Base Policy, which is authorised to hold equity. Whether the Pentagon has the legal authority to act in this way is debatable; it is up to Congress to consider the matter. The Trump administration appears to have used a financial tool called “penny warrants” to structure its equity stake. In any event, the Trump administration appears to have used a financial tool called “penny warrants” to structure its equity stake. This instrument would give the U.S. the opportunity to purchase stock in NABEP for a nominal price at a certain point in the future, an arrangement that could give Washington a steep discount once the stock appreciates, entitle it to dividends and afford it substantial control of the company’s future. Under the Trump administration, the Pentagon has expanded the precedent of using these warrants when making loans, allowing the government to later sell them, potentially for a profit – operating, in effect, like a venture capital firm. The opacity of the deal, along with suspicions that certain private-sector interests are being favoured thanks to their government ties in Caracas, Washington or both, have stirred additional concerns. The U.S. Congress was on legislative recess at the time of the announcement, and reactions, mostly on social media, have split largely along party lines, with Republicans generally supportive and Democrats flagging concerns. Florida Republicans, who are up for re-election in districts with large Venezuelan diaspora communities, were somewhat cautious, emphasising the need for free and fair elections. On the other hand, Democrats who have been sceptical of the administration’s aims in Venezuela have criticised the deal on grounds of potential corruption . Among other issues, NABEP is run by Alejandro Betancourt, a Venezuelan businessman who has faced multiple investigations at home and abroad for alleged embezzlement of Venezuelan state funds and is linked to Rodríguez’s government (more below). What does the U.S. administration want from this deal? The agreement comes at a time when President Trump is facing declining poll numbers , criticism of his handling of foreign policy ( in particular his conduct of the Middle East war) and growing concerns about his economic management. Voters worry about the cost of living, especially fuel prices, with diesel hitting a new record high, surging over 55 per cent since the war began. According to the latest polling, Democrats are in contention to win control of both the House and the Senate in midterm elections, which are widely seen as a referendum on Trump’s second term. Faced with these political headwinds, Trump has returned to his long-running fixation with “taking the oil” in his approach to U.S. foreign relations. (One of Trump’s critiques of the 2003 Iraq war was precisely that the U.S. did not assume control of the country’s fossil fuels.) The administration has boasted that this deal will secure “U.S. energy dominance for the next century” and even boost the country’s economic growth, as the crude would be “processed through U.S. refineries and pumped with American rigs and infrastructure”. The oil derived from the agreement would, according to the White House , supply the military and serve “other sensitive uses”. In the long run, it could also theoretically provide barrels for the U.S. consumer market and allow domestic production to refill the country’s strategic oil reserve, which is now at its lowest point since 1983. The agreement with Venezuela, however, may fail to meet these sunny predictions of a spurt in oil production. While the fields assigned to NABEP supposedly represent 65 billion barrels of recoverable oil, the figure is based on a highly optimistic 20 per cent recovery rate, the term for what portion of the oil in a given deposit can reasonably be extracted over its lifetime. According to Venezuelan oil specialist Francisco Monaldi, the true figure is likely nearer one third of that. (If the higher estimates are correct, Saudi Aramco would be the only private company in the world controlling larger oil reserves than NABEP, according to U.S. officials.) Economists are in broad agreement that Venezuela’s oil industry would need tens of billions of dollars in investment ... to restore production to historical levels. Moreover, any major increase in Venezuelan oil production would not be achieved in the near future – and certainly not before the U.S. midterm elections. Venezuela currently produces between 800,000 and 900,000 barrels a day, compared to over three million barrels a day in the first decade of the 21st century. NABEP is pumping about 200,000 barrels per day, and Washington appears to have chosen Betancourt as a partner precisely because he has the contacts and risk tolerance to advance difficult projects. Yet even the rosiest projections, assuming rapid efforts to rehabilitate existing oilfields and infrastructure, suggest that a minimum of two years will be required before the deal will generate new streams of revenue. Around half the identified potential projects involve “greenfield” or undeveloped sites, some of them “in the middle of nowhere”, as an oil company representative told Crisis Group. Economists are in broad agreement that Venezuela’s oil industry would need tens of billions of dollars in investment and nearly a decade of work to restore production to historical levels. Since the U.S. government says it will not be putting up the money (as noted, the administration has stressed that the deal is cost-free for U.S. taxpayers), and the only private company so far involved, NABEP, does not have it, it remains unclear where that investment will come from. The Washington Post reported that Betancourt may seek advance payments from oil traders up front, based on anticipated later revenue. But major oil corporations seem unlikely to work with NABEP directly, given the judicial cases against Betancourt and concerns about the agreement’s legality in Venezuela. A number of them, however, have been negotiating their own concessions with the Rodríguez government, focusing either on gas or on the expansion of existing operations. Chevron Corporation, which remained in Venezuela while many others left, announced on 2 September that it would work through its Venezuelan joint ventures to develop new fields adjacent to its existing operations, with the aim of doubling its Venezuela output to 600,000 barrels a day over the next five years, according to the oil firm . After 3 January, the U.S. gave commodity traders Vitol Group and Trafigura Group the contracts to place Venezuelan oil on the international market, though soon afterward Washington opened the business to other traders. More recently, several refiners have begun to deal directly with the Venezuelan state oil corporation PDVSA, bypassing the middlemen. Beyond the oil itself, the administration describes the deal as “reasserting the Monroe Doctrine”, which it understands as ensuring U.S. hegemony in the Western Hemisphere. So far, its efforts to cement U.S. dominance have included cultivating political allies, boosting its stakes in the region’s natural resources and critical minerals, and encouraging regional military cooperation aimed at stemming the flows of drugs and migrants northward. As part of the latter, a campaign against small boats allegedly trafficking narcotics on both the Pacific and Caribbean seaboards, deemed by a critical mass of legal scholars to involve extrajudicial killings, had claimed at least 227 lives as of early September . Trump’s application of the doctrine is also explicit in seeking to push other global powers out of positions of influence in Latin America. The White House says NABEP would operate oilfields previously controlled or serviced by Russian and Chinese firms. In response, the Chinese government demanded that its “legitimate rights and interests” be respected. Beijing is still believed to be owed over $10 billion from past credit offered Venezuela; this debt was largely being paid in kind, through oil shipments, before 3 January. Russia has previously decried what a Kremlin spokesman called “blatant discrimination” against it, and in February the Russian state-owned oil company Roszarubezhneft promised to defend its legal claims. What do Venezuelans think? Criticism, much of it impassioned, has come from across the political spectrum. Venezuelans have questioned not only the ties with NABEP, but also the deal’s lack of transparency and the fact that it was announced without input from the Venezuelan people and in the absence of legitimately elected authorities. Even those inclined to support the arrangement concede that it is hard to defend without full disclosure of its terms. Many ordinary Venezuelans have told Crisis Group of their shock and dismay at the public statements describing its parameters. Left-wing opponents of the Rodríguez government, who argue that the interim president is betraying the legacy of the founder of the ruling chavista movement, former President Chávez, staged a small but noisy march in central Caracas on 29 August to protest the deal. Chávez’s long-time oil minister Rafael Ramírez, who is exiled in Italy and faces corruption allegations (which he denies) back home, called it a “neocolonial” arrangement and a “ dagger to the heart ” of Venezuela. Economists associated with both the moderate and hard-line wings of the opposition also questioned the deal. Harvard professor Ricardo Hausmann, a former Venezuelan planning minister and supporter of exiled opposition leader María Corina Machado, called it “ shameful ” and “illegitimate”. Machado herself was initially silent. While she has expressed her support for the Trump administration’s intervention in Venezuela and long championed the full privatisation of the oil industry, she and her movement Vente Venezuela have not challenged the concept of state ownership of oil reserves; they have instead insisted that any restructuring of the industry be carried out by a democratically elected government. On 3 September, Machado broke her silence, releasing a seven-minute video in which she describes the “sadness [and] anger” the announcement provoked, and spoke of “deep concern” about its implications, though without mentioning Trump by name. The chequered history of NABEP’s owner, Alejandro Betancourt, is a particular source of concern. Few if any private individuals are more closely associated in the minds of Venezuelans with the alleged embezzlement of public funds than Betancourt. As a young businessman, he founded Derwick Associates, which in 2011 obtained a series of no-bid contracts worth around $5 billion to build power stations amid a nationwide electricity shortage. The company appears to have taken the up-front payments but failed to resolve the problem; Venezuela today suffers from its most severe blackouts ever. Amid this cacophony of objections, the opposition team hand-picked by Washington for political transition talks with the Rodríguez government, led by 2015 National Assembly chair Dinorah Figuera, has found it hard to respond publicly. Neither Figuera’s faction nor Machado’s seems to have been consulted on the deal before it was made public. Is the deal legal? Several aspects of the agreement appear to run afoul of Venezuelan law. While the reported arrangement includes a 100-year concession, Article 12 of the country’s constitution declares the country’s oil deposits public property, and as such inalienable, while Article 302 grants the state the exclusive right to exploit them. Even under the sweeping oil law reform that came into force earlier in 2026, private ownership (as opposed to operational control) of an oilfield is not allowed, and an initial concession cannot exceed 25 years. In her public statements, Rodríguez has insisted that the agreement in no way infringes upon Venezuela’s sovereign rights, without offering details. Another source of legal jeopardy is the status of the Rodríguez government itself. The acting president, who has never held elected office, owes her position to the 3 January U.S. military incursion that ousted Maduro and installed her in power. Venezuela’s parliament, the National Assembly – which endorsed the oil accord on 1 September without having seen the full text – is chaired by Rodríguez’s brother Jorge and largely acts as a rubber stamp for the executive. (Opposition legislators of the small Libertad caucus abstained from voting on the agreement, saying they needed to see the actual text.) The U.S. government has described the 2025 legislative elections as a “sham”. Indeed, the Trump administration continues to recognise the rump of the opposition-dominated 2016-2021 parliament (known as the 2015 Assembly, for the year it was elected) as the only surviving democratic institution in the country. Under the Venezuelan constitution, the acts of any official or branch of the state considered to have “usurped” authority are rendered null and void. The eventual restoration of constitutional normality and the rule of law in Venezuela would thus open the very real possibility of a legal challenge to the agreement, even if a new government was not opposed to the deal. What does this mean for Venezuela’s future? Since the 3 January raid, the Trump administration has assumed a dominant role in determining Venezuela’s political and economic trajectory, with the U.S. president even suggesting that it could become the 51st state. Washington’s stranglehold on the country’s foreign earnings, and the explicit threat of further military action if Caracas defies its will, leave Rodríguez little room for manoeuvre. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has described Washington’s three-phase plan for Venezuela as involving stabilisation, economic recovery and political transition. Yet far from pushing for a fresh presidential election to make amends for the last poll fraudulently won by Maduro in July 2024, Trump has repeatedly expressed his satisfaction with the current set-up, describing Rodríguez as “highly respected” and giving her government glowing praise. In late July, Trump declared that Venezuela was “ not ready yet ” for elections. With terms that appear designed to favour U.S. interests over those of Venezuelans, which depend on Caracas’s compliance, and which would likely prove unacceptable to a freely elected government, this deal further reduces the incentives for the White House to seek democratic change in Venezuela. The deal also complicates efforts by the opposition to push for a genuine political transition. Washington has compelled the Rodríguez government to sit down to talks with an opposition delegation led by Dinorah Figuera on political reform. Those talks began in August, producing an initial agreement on change at the Supreme Court. Negotiations are due to resume in mid-September, with a focus on political rights and reform of the electoral authority. But the opposition delegation representing the 2015 Assembly has little leverage beyond its U.S. backing. It already suffers from a perceived deficit of legitimacy, and its reputation may be further tarnished by association with an unpopular deal that the delegation was not consulted on but may lack the autonomy to repudiate. Machado is also in a bind. She has repeatedly sought to return to Venezuela, only to be blocked by the Trump-Rodríguez alliance. Neither confrontation with Trump nor blind obedience will further Machado’s calls for a quick and free presidential vote that would likely cement her status as pre-eminent opposition leader and might see her emerge victorious. In her video message about the deal, Machado reiterated that she views the U.S. as “the principal partner Venezuela needs” but added that agreements of this magnitude require “solid institutions”, not arbitrary assignations. She repeated her call for free elections as soon as possible. Some Venezuelans say they would be prepared to accept the loss of sovereignty in exchange for greater political freedom and an improvement in economic conditions. Some Venezuelans say they would be prepared to accept the loss of sovereignty in exchange for greater political freedom and an improvement in economic conditions for a country that has been mired in a humanitarian emergency for well over a decade. Needs have only grown more acute following twin earthquakes in June that the UN estimates added 700,000 individuals to the list of those in need of basic assistance. But neither freedom nor economic relief appear guaranteed within the compass of the current arrangement between Caracas and Washington. More broadly, the overall terms of the post-3 January relationship between the U.S. and Venezuela give serious cause for concern. Washington’s direct control of key pieces of Venezuela’s economy and its outsized influence over its government have led Caracas to loosen its shackles on political dissent but have also created a set of perverse incentives that seem to be hindering progress toward a genuine democratic opening. Venezuela’s politicians and business leaders are obliged to appeal first and foremost to the Trump administration rather than to any domestic constituency. Trump, meanwhile, has made quite explicit his view that the Venezuela operation is a blueprint for Latin America and beyond, combining military force, economic coercion and resource extraction. Regardless of whether administration officials still imagine a medium- to long-term plan for a democratic transition, for now Washington appears determined to grab what it can before Venezuelans can once more exercise their right to govern themselves.
