An Historic Poll Puts Peace to the Test in the Philippines cthuratong Fri, 09/11/2026 - 17:10 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Campaign posters in Cotabato City, in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, Philippines. August 2026. CRISIS GROUP / Georgi Engelbrecht Q&A / Asia-Pacific 11 September 2026 12 minutes An Historic Poll Puts Peace to the Test in the Philippines In mid-September, residents of the Bangsamoro in the southern Philippines will elect regional parliamentary representatives. In this Q&A, Crisis Group expert Georgi Engelbrecht explains the importance of this step in the peace process between the national government and ex-rebels in the region. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Georgi Engelbrecht Senior Analyst, Philippines https://twitter.com/Durian_Diaries Related Tags Philippines What is happening? On 14 September, over two million residents of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao will elect their parliament for the first time. The vote is a milestone in the implementation of the 2014 peace accord, which ended decades of conflict between the Philippine government and Moro Muslim separatists. In 2019, a parliament was created to govern the Bangsamoro, with Philippine presidents appointing its members. Slightly more than half the seats were reserved for members of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, or MILF, the region’s largest Moro Muslim armed movement. Following four postponements of the vote over the last seven years – first because of the COVID-19 pandemic, and later due to a range of legal and political complications – residents will finally have the chance to elect all their regional parliamentary representatives. The fact that the vote is now taking place is an accomplishment in and of itself. Election fever has gripped the region since the campaign officially began in late July. Vehicles roam the streets with loudspeakers blasting party jingles, huge posters of candidates decorate Bangsamoro roads, and catchy slogans and vlogs saturate citizens’ social media feeds. With voters set to choose from twelve parties, and with 631 candidates jockeying for 80 parliamentary seats, the competition to attract public support has been fierce. Electioneering has a darker side, too, with some campaigns spreading disinformation about rival candidates and parties. The vote is set to deliver a long-awaited verdict on how well MILF candidates have handled the transition from conducting guerrilla warfare to administering the autonomous region. Over the last seven years, the MILF-led interim administration has achieved a number of modest results, for instance strengthening social services and reducing child mortality. That said, and despite residents’ high expectations at the start of the peace process, the people of the Bangsamoro are still among the poorest in the country. The elections also come at a moment of high tension within the movement’s ranks. In March 2025, the national government replaced Chief Minister Murad Ebrahim, the MILF’s chairman, with the movement’s top military commander Abdulraof Macacua, generating a schism in the organisation. During an assembly in early September, the Central Committee stripped Macacua and 40 other MILF military commanders of their official functions. Mohagher Iqbal, head of the peace implementation panel and MILF vice chair, remains loyal to the displaced chief minister, Murad. Who is taking part in the polls? Twelve political parties are competing. While some have laid out clear platforms, the majority have had little of substance to offer in their campaigns. Such is often the case in the Philippines, where political campaigns tend to centre around personalities, rather than policy platforms, given the weaknesses of the party system. Even so, a milestone in the Bangsamoro’s political life came on 27 August, when representatives from all parties took part in a six-hour public debate in Cotabato City on priorities for the future government. Broadly speaking, the political spectrum can be divided into three blocs. The first is made up of the ex-rebels, who are represented by three parties broadly reflecting the split at the heights of the MILF: the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP), which is a vehicle for Murad; the Bangsamoro Federalist Party, which is led by Macacua but includes several senior MILF cadres and influential local politicians; and the ABOT party, which is comprised of Iqbal partisans. In addition to the troika of parties affiliated with the MILF, two parties have emerged from the Moro National Liberation Front, the Bangsamoro’s first separatist movement (from which the MILF split in 1977). Campaign posters of the United Bangsamoro Justice Party in Cotabato City, in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, Philippines. August 2026. CRISIS GROUP / Georgi Engelbrecht The second category consists of parties led by the region’s political clans, or families that dominate local politics and aspire to extend their reach across the region. The most notable is the Bangsamoro Grand Coalition, an alliance of powerful clan leaders associated with the Alonto-Adiong, Hataman and Mangudadatu families, whose members felt politically excluded during the MILF-led interim administration. Once the primary opposition to the ex-rebels, this coalition now faces competition from the Bangsamoro Federalist Party mentioned above, as well as the Progressive Bangsamoro Party, whose base is in the provinces of Sulu and Tawi-Tawi. The latter is linked to the Loong and Matba families. A third category encompasses smaller parties. Some of these are led by civil society figures who promise institutional reform and champion minority rights. The Raayat Party, for example, includes experienced lawyers and legislators who are pressing for transparency in government and better access to public services. The Indigenous, Settler, Sama and Minorities Alliance Party, which focuses on safeguarding the rights and interests of the region’s Sama minority, is also among the smaller parties that would bring valuable expertise and perspectives to the parliament. These two parties are, however, unlikely to win more than a handful of seats . Half the parliamentary seats will be filled via proportional representation, with voters casting ballots for party lists. Citizens across the region’s 32 electoral districts will also vote for district representatives, who will fill another 40 per cent of the seats. The remaining 10 per cent (eight seats) are reserved for “sectors”, also elected by popular vote – except in the case of non-Moro Indigenous communities, whose representatives have already been elected via community assemblies . Non-Moro Indigenous communities and Christian settlers will each hold two seats, while women, traditional leaders, youth and religious scholars (known as ulama ) will have one seat each. Once the elected parliamentarians take office on 30 October, they will elect the chief minister through a majority vote. Unless a single party wins more than 41 seats – an unlikely prospect – party leaders will therefore need to forge a coalition in order to form a government. Some locals suspect that President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr.’s administration favours an outcome that would preserve Macacua as leader, with his MILF faction governing in a coalition with dominant local clans. This suspicion is not unfounded, given the national government’s unexpected move in 2025 to place Macacua at the helm of the Bangsamoro government. Campaign posters of the Bangsamoro Federalist Party and the Bangsamoro Party in Cotabato City, in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, Philippines. August 2026. CRISIS GROUP / Georgi Engelbrecht How has the campaign played out? The UBJP has campaigned hard. Its strategy consists of harnessing grassroots support while building alliances with politicians who oppose the Grand Coalition and the Federalist Party. Leaders and senior cadres emphasise the importance of honouring the 2014 peace agreement in full. In rallies across the region, UBJP candidates have called for “moral governance”, a concept that infuses the notion of good governance with Islamic principles. Other parties also invoke religious language, but the UBJP is the only one using it as a pillar of its campaign. The Federalist Party, meanwhile, has focused on a message of “inclusion” and anti-corruption, while the parties associated with the MNLF highlight their movement’s early contribution to the Moro struggle. The Grand Coalition, for its part, is leveraging its clan-based network, which is led by the governors of Lanao del Sur and Basilan. The campaign has revealed an inherent contradiction at the heart of Bangsamoro politics. That is, despite the establishment of a parliamentary system – which is distinct from the presidential system used by the Philippines at the national level – and the concomitant creation of new political parties, clans and personalities still matter more than parties or issues. Established political families can leverage patronage, largesse and the campaign experience they have acquired thanks to national and local polls to garner voters’ support. Familial ties still shape party lists, and some clans are fielding candidates from different parties in order to ensure that they are installed in the region’s power structure no matter the vote’s outcome. “The electoral game, the innovations of the system, have already been rigged”, a former party aide lamented. Are conditions in place for a peaceful election? Electoral violence constitutes the biggest threat to these polls. Flare-ups are a staple of Philippine politics, and election-related murders are regular occurrences. The presence of armed groups and widespread proliferation of firearms mean that political violence is even more widespread in the Bangsamoro. In the Philippines’ 2025 elections for governors, mayors and national senators, more than a third of the violent incidents recorded nationwide took place in the Bangsamoro. In one incident during the mayoral election in the town of Hadji Mohammad Ajul in Basilan, a clash between warring clans claimed four lives. The Philippine Commission on Elections has designated almost 40 per cent of the region’s towns as being at high risk of violence. Multiple incidents have already occurred since the beginning of the campaign – including an attempted ambush on interim Chief Minister Macacua. It is, however, unclear who was behind the attack. Indeed, many locals believe it may have been staged in order to engender sympathy for Macacua and boost his Federalist Party’s chances. Direct clashes of the military and police with ex-rebels are unlikely, but shootouts and disturbances involving competing political camps and candidates are possible, including on election day. Two main risks stand out. First, contests for district seats – which involve individual candidates facing off against one another – can more easily tip into violence given the personal nature of the competition. Secondly, friction could arise between supporters of the UBJP and the Federalist Party, both of them offshoots of the ex-rebel MILF, as well as between the UBJP and the Grand Coalition, particularly in areas where all the major political forces are campaigning. Those who seek to threaten or attack rivals can deploy tried-and-tested tactics ranging from bombings on the eve of the polls to scare voters to attacks on polling booths. Crisis Group knows of at least one powerbroker who has allegedly prepositioned dozens of rifles in a Maguindanaon village. Inflammatory online posts and trolling, often involving prominent MILF-linked personalities representing different factions, could also help spur real-world violence. A young cadre warned that this escalation is “just a matter of time”. Campaign rhetoric has on occasion turned worryingly bellicose. During a Federalist Party rally in August, Macacua said the party “was prepared for war to ensure that the Bangsamoro is on the right path”. Though he did not specify the target of this warning, some locals perceived it as a threat to his former comrades. On 3 August, top MILF military leader Abdullah Macapaar – alias Commander Bravo, who remains loyal to the Central Committee – warned that opponents of his party might manipulate the polls. The following month, after state authorities intercepted MILF members under his command and sent them back to their camp, he declared in a speech: “If we are picked on, we will not allow ourselves to be bullied”. In terms of potential flashpoints, the greatest security risks lie in the province of Maguindanao del Sur and the Special Geographic Area, a cluster of eight municipalities near the regional capital of Cotabato City. In these locations, candidates include prominent MILF personalities and commanders, as well as traditional elites. For example, the son of MILF chair Murad Ebrahim will face off against Butch Malang, a senior MILF commander widely considered loyal to Chief Minister Macacua. Meanwhile, parts of Lanao del Sur province, which has a long history of political violence, are also vulnerable to flare-ups. The island province of Basilan also warrants close monitoring, given both divisions within the governing Hataman clan and internal MILF rifts. Given how prevalent vote buying is in the Philippines, many locals fear that victory will depend on which political bloc has the most cash to dispense. Whether the elections will be free and fair is another question. Given how prevalent vote buying is in the Philippines, many locals fear that victory will depend on which political bloc has the most cash to dispense. Pre-election assessments highlight this risk, warning that it could undermine the election’s legitimacy. Community leaders Crisis Group spoke to also expressed this view. The practice of command votes, under which influential local leaders tell entire communities whom they should vote for, presents another challenge. While mayors and governors are not running in this election, they have an interest in the fortunes of certain candidates, especially if members of their clans are competing. International and domestic entities are working to promote a free and safe poll. Diplomatic representatives of the European Union, Australia, Switzerland, Singapore and Japan will be present in Cotabato City and a handful of nearby locations. Local and international NGOs such as the Independent Election Monitoring Center in Cotabato City, the Legal Network for Truthful Elections, the International Republican Institute, the National Democratic Institute and the Asia Network for Free Elections , are also deploying across the region. They all aim to publish reports of their findings. The national government, moreover, will be dispatching thousands of soldiers and police to the Bangsamoro, with an eye to deterring election-related violence. Some locals , however, view the deployment as overly heavy-handed. What happens after the vote? The major question hovering over these elections is how the MILF and its various factions will fare. The Bangsamoro electorate already had a chance to vote for UBJP-aligned candidates during the 2022 general and local elections , the 2023 village elections , and the 2025 mid-term and local elections. The party’s performance was not impressive; its few successes relied in no small part on local elite backing (either from mayors or village chairs). The MILF’s internal divisions have weakened the UBJP’s chances even further, since they will splinter the vote for the ex-rebels: this time, many local powerbrokers appear to be siding with the Federalist Party or the Grand Coalition. As a result, the most optimistic forecasts say the UBJP will secure only a quarter of parliamentary seats, at best, and about a tenth at worst. While the party could join with smaller parties to muster a majority, the prospect of it being able to rally enough legislators to make up for a poor performance seems unlikely. A more probable scenario is that the Federalist Party or the Grand Coalition achieves a parliamentary majority, possibly with the support of other parties. Both would then back the election of Macacua as chief minister, though the distribution of ministerial positions would hinge on the vote’s outcome. (Parties that garner more votes will presumably lay claim to a greater share of cabinet appointments.) Whether the UBJP will be able to prevent a clan-based coalition from forming a government with Macacua by driving a wedge between the leading political families, or by persuading elected parliamentarians to defect to its ranks when the vote for chief minister takes place, remains an open question. Not surprisingly, some MILF members still hope for reconciliation among the movement’s leaders, though the prospect of that happening seems slim at this juncture. A major loss for the UBJP would be a significant setback for the MILF’s Central Committee. With the MILF leaders ageing, it would fall to mid-level commanders and cadres to build the party into a credible opposition force in the regional parliament over the next five years. A more immediate concern should the UBJP fare poorly is the potential for conflict. Should the MILF rank and file loyal to Murad come to believe that Macacua conspired with Manila to strip the UBJP of its win, aggrieved fighters might turn their frustrations on their former comrades or the national government. The MILF itself could also withdraw from official peace process activities and refuse to disarm. It could even dispatch its troops back to the region’s hills and jungles to express its frustration without resorting to fighting. While successful elections are a crucial step in the peace process, much of the agreement remains unrealised. While successful elections are a crucial step in the peace process, much of the agreement remains unrealised. Rebel and militia demobilisation are stuck in bureaucratic limbo. Manila has pledged to convert former MILF camps into “safe and prosperous communities” by building infrastructure such as roads and starting community-managed economic projects. That effort also lags behind schedule. The same is true of the accord’s transitional justice and amnesty provisions. The government and the peace panel of MILF’s Central Committee, which is aligned with the UBJP and has been in charge of the peace process for the former rebels, have agreed to meet in the Malaysian capital Kuala Lumpur after the vote to discuss implementation of the remaining points of the peace agreement. That might be a sign that Manila is committed to honouring the accord no matter how the elections turn out. Still, there is a growing risk that President Marcos, Jr. will not make the peace process a priority as his term in office starts to wind down. Should the MILF Central Committee’s influence further erode as the splits between ex-rebels widen, Manila may also see little reason to continue treating the movement as an equal partner. For residents of the Bangsamoro, meanwhile, the new regional administration will need to leverage its electoral legitimacy to institute policies that make a material difference in their lives. They are still anxiously waiting for the changes the peace deal promised to start delivering over a decade ago. Ten Challenges for the UN in 2026-2027 eschelhaas Mon, 09/14/2026 - 10:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Candidates for United Nations Secretary-General position participate in a debate at the UN General Assembly Hall in New York, on July 23, 2026. Leonardo MUNOZ / AFP Special Briefing 15 / Multilateral Diplomacy 14 September 2026 20+ minutes Ten Challenges for the UN in 2026-2027 As the 2026 General Assembly begins, the UN remains hobbled by cost cutting and big-power wrangling. The new Secretary-General to be chosen soon cannot cure all that ails the organisation, but much can be done to put its still considerable capacity to work. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print "> Download PDF Full Report (en) Related Tags Global What’s new? Leaders gathering at the UN General Assembly will find an organisation in need of revival. UN diplomacy aimed at halting wars and easing civilian suffering remains paralysed, while funding cuts have weakened UN capacity. States have one eye to the future as they prepare to appoint a new Secretary-General. Why does it matter? The UN remains the only universal forum for global cooperation on war and peace, even as the international order it anchors is under mounting strain. Many member states hope the next Secretary-General can help the organisation dispel its malaise and forge a new direction. What should be done? A new Secretary-General cannot resolve the world’s crises overnight, but this person should work with member states to address immediate challenges. High on the list should be bolstering the UN’s peacemaking and conflict management capabilities, mobilising political and financial support, and making a renewed case for international cooperation. I. Overview When world leaders last met at the UN General Assembly in September 2025, the organisation was in disarray, reeling from U.S. aid freezes and major-power disputes. A year on, the organisation remains trapped in an open-ended crisis, even after an additional round of cost cutting and other reforms. Under the Trump administration, the U.S. has morphed from a flawed champion of the international legal order into an overt scofflaw. While the U.S. has not repudiated the multilateral system anchored by the UN, it has done great damage to the organisation, insisting on shrinking multilateral peace operations, slow-rolling funding and tried to impose its ideological agenda. The Security Council continues to be a forum for hashing out big-power differences – with the U.S., Russia and China coming to agreement on second-tier files. But as regards the most salient peace and security challenges today – the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, as well as Ukraine and Sudan – the UN is notable mainly for being stuck. The next Secretary-General cannot cure all that ails the UN, but creative diplomacy could be useful in putting its still considerable capacity to work. If the overall mood at the UN is one of drifting toward perdition, it is partly because everyone is waiting for change at the top of the system. Secretary-General António Guterres will complete his term at the end of December. A small batch of candidates – eight, at the time of writing – have been publicly and privately lobbying throughout the year to replace him. Most have been cautious in their campaigning, to avoid offending the major powers that dominate the selection process. UN insiders are watching with mixed feelings. Some hope that the next Secretary-General can bring new energy to the organisation and, assuming Washington is amenable, restore a measure of political relevance and financial stability. Others worry that the U.S., China and Russia will connive to choose a weak candidate firmly under their control and that the Trump administration will force the next UN chief to make even more radical cuts throughout the institution. The selection process has at least focused minds on what the UN, multilateral cooperation and international law exist to achieve. Many member states have emphasised that they would like to see the incoming Secretary-General do more to promote conflict prevention and resolution, which Guterres has sometimes given short shrift while pursuing other goals, such as international cooperation on artificial intelligence. Guterres no doubt felt that he had little to gain by focusing on geopolitical crises given the lack of consensus among the big powers. But there is now a widespread sense that the UN cannot pretend to be a useful platform for discussions of far-reaching issues like AI if governments do not believe that it can deliver on its core, UN Charter-defined purpose of maintaining peace and security. The crises of the last twelve months have also offered reminders of the extent to which the UN still offers a necessary if imperfect scaffolding for international cooperation. The Trump administration has grudgingly turned to the Security Council to endorse its conflict management efforts in Haiti and Gaza. Faced with the fallout of the U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran, such as closure of the Strait of Hormuz, governments around the world have stressed the importance of international legal principles including the prohibition of aggressive war, rules protecting civilians and civilian objects in conflict, and freedom of navigation. Though the UN has had a vanishingly small voice in diplomacy aimed at ending the Middle East war, both U.S. and Iranian officials have acknowledged that the Security Council should play some role – if only a ministerial one – in any peace deal. The UN ... remains best positioned to deliver humanitarian aid, mount peace operations and manage protracted crises that few other actors ... can handle. These are small consolations, but at a moment in which the U.S. and Russia are learning the limits of hard power in the Middle East and Ukraine, there is still space to reiterate the case for diplomacy, cooperation and respect for law. The next UN Secretary-General can make it. While it is foolish to expect a single administrator, however senior, to save the world, many small and midsize UN member states, as well as many major-power officials, are ready to heed a call to reinforce the lapsing international legal order. The UN also remains best positioned to deliver humanitarian aid, mount peace operations and manage protracted crises that few other actors – including the flailing U.S.-backed Board of Peace – can handle. It is possible that new leadership at the UN can give the organisation as a whole, and its peace and security pillar in particular, a new strategic direction. But amid deadly violence, regional rifts and institutional headaches, it is a near certainty that UN crisis management will continue to involve a great deal of firefighting and muddling through. This briefing, based on Crisis Group’s research at the UN and in the countries concerned, offers a guide to some of the most urgent issues. II. The Year in Review: Trends in UN Diplomacy The UN spent much of the past year adapting to a more assertive and transactional U.S. administration. Alongside long-running crises in Ukraine, Gaza and Sudan, the latest U.S.-Israeli war with Iran placed additional strain on Council diplomacy and the UN-backed international order. 1 Crisis Group Special Briefing N°14, Causes of Peace in an Era of Hard Power , 8 July 2026. Meanwhile, the UN’s multi-year liquidity crisis worsened, compounded by the U.S. aid cuts, disrupting operations at headquarters in New York and in the field. Steep reductions in voluntary contributions to UN humanitarian agencies forced the organisation to make difficult choices with its assistance, leaving many civilians affected by armed conflict with little support. Debates over the UN’s future simmered as member states began their search for the next Secretary-General. A year after Donald Trump’s return to the White House, the organisation was no longer in shock but adjusting to a new normal. A. Crisis Management and UN Diplomacy 1. The Security Council A year ago, Crisis Group observed that U.S. diplomacy at the Security Council under the newly installed Trump administration had lacked a clear direction. 2 Crisis Group Special Briefing N°13, Ten Challenges for the UN in 2025-2026 , 9 September 2025. The arrival of U.S. Ambassador Mike Waltz in New York on the eve of the 2025 UN General Assembly marked the beginning of a more purposeful, and often determined, U.S. approach in the Council. Together with Panama, the U.S. secured Council authorisation for a new Gang Suppression Force for Haiti shortly after Waltz’s arrival, along with a UN logistics office to defray some of the Force’s costs (see Section III.4). 3 “ Haiti: Vote on a Draft Resolution Authorizing a ‘Gang Suppression Force’ and a UN Support Office* ”, Security Council Report, 30 September 2025; Daniel Forti, “ New Force to Battle Haiti’s Gangs Gets Security Council Blessing ”, Crisis Group Analyst’s Notebook, 1 October 2025; Crisis Group Latin America & Caribbean Report N°110, Undoing Haiti’s Deadly Gang Alliance , 15 December 2025. Less than two months later, the Trump administration – backed by its regional partners and Palestine – persuaded the Council to endorse its ceasefire plan for Gaza and establish the vaguely defined Board of Peace. 4 “Resolution 2803”, UNSC S/RES/2803, 17 November 2025; Daniel Forti, Richard Gowan and Max Rodenbeck, “ What to Look for as the Gaza Peace Plan Comes to the UN Security Council ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 14 November 2025. In both cases, the Council agreed to arrangements that concentrated decision-making authority in Washington and minimised the UN’s political and operational roles. With UN diplomacy on the war in Gaza lowered to a simmer (see Section III.3), the U.S.-Iran conflict became the Council’s defining crisis of the past year. Major-power tensions over Iran were already high at the UN prior to the outbreak of hostilities at the end of February. After the breakdown of nuclear diplomacy between the U.S. and Iran in 2025 and the twelve-day campaign launched by Israel (and joined by the U.S.) against Iran in June, France, Germany and the UK – three of the participants in the 2015 nuclear deal, or Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action – decided to reimpose “snapback” sanctions on Tehran that were otherwise set to expire that October. 5 Naysan Rafati and Daniel Forti, “ Iran Sanctions Snapback at the UN ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 25 August 2026. Beijing and Moscow rejected the legality of the reimposed UN sanctions, and in protest, they have obstructed business in all of the Council’s sanctions committees and thematic working groups since 2026 began. 6 China and Russia have blocked the appointment of the chairs and vice chairs of all subsidiary bodies, which require Council unanimity according to the body’s informal working methods. The chairs and vice chairs are responsible for leading each body’s meetings, briefing the Council on behalf of each body and managing its workflow. For more, see “ In Hindsight: A Second Year of Delays in the Allocation of Subsidiary Body Chairs ”, Security Council Report, 1 July 2026; Letter from the Security Council’s ten elected members , UNSC S/2026/636, 30 July 2026. Tensions in the Council gradually escalated after the U.S. and Israel once again attacked Iran on 28 February. Tensions in the Council gradually escalated after the U.S. and Israel once again attacked Iran on 28 February. China and Russia sharply criticised the two states during the Council’s first emergency meeting on the war. But even so they allowed passage of a Bahrain-led resolution condemning Iran’s retaliatory fire at its Gulf Arab neighbours days later, abstaining instead of vetoing it. Their posture suggested that preserving relations with the Gulf states was a higher priority than blocking a one-sided resolution that had no teeth. 7 Beijing and Moscow abstained from the vote. Russia also submitted a separate counter-resolution discussing the war’s root causes that got too few votes to be adopted. See “ Resolution 2817 ”, UNSC S/RES/2817, 11 March 2026. Their stances gradually hardened, however, as Washington pressed the Security Council to consider more coercive measures against Tehran. In early April, the Gulf states and the U.S. tabled a resolution for the Council to endorse a vaguely defined multinational naval coalition that would be tasked with reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Moscow and Beijing vetoed the text despite intense lobbying by Gulf capitals, arguing that the resolution would have given the U.S. open-ended authorisation to escalate its campaign. 8 The vote took place hours after U.S. President Donald Trump shared a social media message threatening to annihilate Iran. During its explanation of vote, Russia invoked the Security Council’s 2011 open-ended authorisation of NATO-led military action in Libya as a comparison to the proposed Gulf-U.S. initiative. Despite finding over 138 co-sponsors, the U.S. and Bahrain did not submit the text for a vote, as they could not secure the support of Russia and China. Council diplomacy on the file has since stalled. Complex and sometimes volatile relations among the U.S., China, and Russia continue to shape the boundaries of Council diplomacy beyond the Gulf. After the reversal of U.S. Ukraine policy in early 2025, when the Trump administration stopped sending arms to Kyiv to resist Russia’s all-out invasion, Moscow may have expected Washington to press the Ukrainian government to make concessions in negotiations to end the fighting. Instead, U.S. statements in the Security Council have criticised Russia’s full-scale invasion and called on the Kremlin to agree to an immediate ceasefire. 9 Remarks by the United States, “ Provisional Verbatim of the 10166th Meeting of the United Nations Security Council ”, UNSC S/PV.10166, 8 June 2026. More often than not, U.S. and Russian diplomats have sparred over UN responses to crises in the Middle East and Africa. Though they frequently clash, recent Council action has depended on a degree of cooperation between these geopolitical rivals. In September 2025, the U.S. agreed to pay nearly $680 million to the UN peacekeeping budget and drop its objections to China becoming penholder on the Council’s Afghanistan file in exchange for Beijing’s support for the Gang Suppression Force in Haiti. 10 Daniel Forti and Richard Gowan, “ Reading the Signals of China’s U.N. As for UN peace operations, where Washington sees clear strategic interests at stake, such as in the DRC and South Sudan, it has been willing to preserve UN missions and, at times, moderate its normally reflexive opposition to human rights, gender and climate-related activities – including where it has been stubborn in other mandate negotiations in the Security Council and General Assembly. The Secretary-General Secretary-General Guterres has spent much of his final year in office trying to forestall the UN’s urgent financial crisis (discussed below), complete reforms under the UN80 initiative that he launched in 2025 and defend the UN Charter in response to violations by two permanent members, Russia and the U.S. 21 The UN80 initiative, launched by Guterres in March 2025, is premised on three separate reform processes. The first is premised on budget cuts and cost savings at the UN Secretariat; the second features a review of all inter-governmental mandates; and the third is anchored in proposals for larger institutional reforms (including proposals to merge different UN agencies and offices). “ UN80 Initiative ”, UN, August 2026. Neither Moscow nor Washington is eager to engage with him personally, curtailing his opportunities to pursue new diplomatic efforts. But the Secretary-General’s cautious outlook toward UN-led conflict management has left many diplomats and officials searching for a successor who will put the organisation’s work on peace and security front and centre. The Secretary-General’s limited influence over the past year has not always been due to a lack of initiative. Shortly after the resumption of hostilities between the U.S. and Iran, Guterres appealed for creating a humanitarian corridor to permit the passage of fuel and fertiliser through the Strait of Hormuz, established a UN mechanism modelled on the Black Sea Grain Initiative to facilitate these efforts and appointed a personal envoy to boost the UN’s diplomatic response. 22 “ Note to Correspondents: on the Strait of Hormuz ”, UN, 27 March 2026. His focus on the war’s global consequences won plaudits but failed to have meaningful impact, as neither the Gulf states nor the U.S. showed serious interest in reopening the strait, except in full and without condition. The initiative has faded from memory even as the war has reignited and traffic through the waterway remains constrained. 23 Guterres shared a brief update about the UN mechanism at a 24 August press conference. See “ Secretary-General’s Press Encounter – On the United Nations’ Efforts to Uphold Navigational Rights and Freedoms ”, Office of the UN Secretary-General, 24 August 2026. Elsewhere, Guterres has deployed his dwindling political capital selectively. At the end of July, he travelled to Cyprus to revive his long-running mediation between Greek and Turkish Cypriots. He also made personal appeals to Sudan’s belligerents in support of a proposed humanitarian ceasefire in Darfur. The Secretary-General continued to press for Security Council reform, including at a high-level summit convened by France and Kenya in May, and in August he released a long-awaited review of UN peace operations mandated by the 2024 Pact for the Future (see Section III.9). 24 “ Review on the future of all forms of United Nations Peace Operations ”, UNGA A/80/798 – UNSC S/2026/600, 22 July 2026. Yet meaningful progress on these and other such priorities has eluded him. B. UN Reform The UN’s financial outlook has deteriorated sharply over the past year, largely due to Washington’s failure to pay its fair share. Since President Trump returned to office, the U.S. has ponied up only a portion of the nearly $4 billion in dues it owes the organisation. 25 In late August, the U.S. agreed to make a payment of $725 million to the UN regular budget, an amount reportedly calculated by Washington to avoid losing its vote in the General Assembly under Article 19 of the UN Charter. The U.S. is not the only member state withholding its obligatory dues, even if it is the largest and has accumulated the most arrears. China has regularly delayed its annual payments to the UN regular budget – in 2026 paying only at the beginning of September – though it traditionally does not accumulate arrears. See Catherine Pollard, “ Financial situation of the United Nations ”, statement to the Fifth Committee of the General Assembly at its 80th Session, 7 May 2026; “ Chandramouli Ramanathan (UN Controller) & others on the UN Budget ”, Office of the UN Spokesperson, 1 July 2026; Humeyra Pamuk and Emma Farge, “ US plans $725 million payment towards its large UN debt ”, Reuters, 21 August 2026. U.S. officials have openly stated their intention to place the UN on a starvation diet and withdrawn from several UN bodies. 26 “ Withdrawing the United States from International Organizations, Conventions and Treaties that Are Contrary to the Interests of the United States ”, White House, 7 January 2026; Emma Farge, Olivia Le Poidevin, Simon Lewis and David Brunnstrom, “ Diplomatic efforts seek to avert Trump split with UN refugee agency, sources say ”, Reuters, 21 July 2026. C. The Search for a New Secretary-General The process of choosing Guterres’ successor, which began in November 2025, is approaching a crescendo. Members of the Security Council held their first straw poll at the end of July, and they will continue to take these informal soundings until one candidate receives at least nine votes from the fifteen-member body with no objection from any of the five permanent members. Eight candidates are in the running. They are: Ivonne A-Baki (former Ecuadorian ambassador to France and the U.S.), Michelle Bachelet (former president of Chile and head of UN Women), María Fernanda Espinosa Garcés (former foreign minister of Ecuador and president of the 73rd General Assembly), Rafael Grossi (director-general of the International Atomic Energy Agency), Rebeca Grynspan (former second vice president of Costa Rica and head of the UN Conference on Trade and Development), Olara Otunnu (former Ugandan foreign minister and former UN representative for children and armed conflict), Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett (Guyana’s permanent representative to the UN) and Macky Sall (former president of Senegal). 39 María Fernanda Espinosa Garcés currently serves on Crisis Group’s Board of Trustees. Ten Challenges for the UN Even as the UN is mired in interlocking difficulties, the organisation can still contribute to conflict resolution and crisis management in many domains. The following list features countries and issue areas where the UN confronts either major challenges or opportunities in the year ahead. It is intended to demonstrate the myriad factors affecting how the UN and its member states respond to conflicts and emergencies around the world. The list is not exhaustive, however, and it excludes cases that Crisis Group has highlighted elsewhere or in years past, such as Afghanistan, the DRC, South Sudan, Ukraine and others. 1. Continuing UN engagement in southern Lebanon In August 2025, the U.S. and Israel strong-armed the Security Council into shutting down the UN peacekeeping mission in southern Lebanon (UNIFIL) – first established in 1978 and significantly upgraded by Resolution 1701 twenty years ago – by the end of 2026 (though the phased withdrawal of troops will extend considerably past 31 December). 50 “ Resolution 2790 ”, UNSC S/RES/2790, 28 August 2025. While questions about southern Lebanon have long vexed the Council, the latest conflagration between Israel and Hizbollah raises the stakes even higher. 51 Heiko Wimmen and David Wood, “ Entrenching a Meaningful Israel-Lebanon Ceasefire ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 19 June 2026. The danger is now that the UN will terminate its 48-year blue helmet operation without clarity on what kind of international presence, if any, might follow. Much will now depend on the trajectory of U.S.-backed negotiations between Israel and Lebanon, which to date have failed to produce a viable security arrangement. The two states signed a “framework agreement” on 26 June, under which the Lebanese army is to assert control of “pilot zones” in southern Lebanon, ensuring that Hizbollah no longer has a military footprint in these areas. 52 “ Trilateral Framework Between the United States of America, the State of Israel and the Republic of Lebanon ”, U.S. Department of State, 26 June 2026. Yet the scheme, which is meant to “serve as the mechanism for phased and verified (Israeli) redeployments”, has already run into trouble. 53 Ibid. Lebanon complains that Israel has kept attacking Lebanese territory, including with lethal airstrikes and the systematic destruction of villages, and authorised “pilot zones” only in areas that it never occupied. Israeli officials, for their part, make Hizbollah’s full disarmament a condition for the Israeli army’s withdrawal. 54 Maayan Lubell and Maya Gebeily, “ After US criticism, Israel ties Lebanon withdrawal to Hezbollah disarmament ”, Reuters, 13 August 2026. Beirut officially outlawed Hizbollah’s military activities in March, but, in practice, it cannot risk trying to compel the group to disarm. 55 Lebanese political and military leaders have resisted calls to deploy the Lebanese army to confront Hizbollah by force. They fear that such a move could trigger disastrous domestic consequences, such as the military fracturing along sectarian lines. Crisis Group Middle East Briefing N°94, Containing Domestic Tensions in War-hit Lebanon , 27 February 2025. See also Michael Young, “ Pushing Beirut into an armed conflict with Hezbollah is insane ”, Diwan (blog), Carnegie Middle East Center, 14 May 2026. Even if the terms of the deal were to be spelled out more precisely, the belligerents would almost certainly refuse to sign up to the underlying bargain. Hizbollah rejects the direct Israel-Lebanon negotiations outright, insisting that Lebanon entrust Iran, the group’s patron, with securing a full Israeli withdrawal as part of Tehran’s negotiations with Washington. 56 “ Hezbollah insists on linking Lebanon to Iran-U.S. negotiations ”, Asharq al-Awsat , 13 July 2026. Though Israel has participated in the trilateral talks with Lebanon and the U.S., it refuses to accept another arrangement like Resolution 1701, under which its troops withdrew from Lebanon after the 2006 war while Hizbollah remained under arms. Debates about a future international presence will also be shaped by U.S. and Israeli scepticism. Israel has long questioned the value of UNIFIL in helping Lebanon constrain Hizbollah, and it has shown little appetite for a replacement that might obstruct its own military operations. The U.S. does not oppose an international mission per se, but it is wary of replicating a UNIFIL model that it deems ineffective. 57 Crisis Group interviews, diplomats and UN officials, Beirut, July 2026. The U.S. and its Israeli partners have long argued that UNIFIL has failed to deter Hizbollah military operations south of the Litani River (even if it has no mandate to confront the militant group by force) and is too expensive. For background, see David Wood, “ Helping UNIFIL Restore Stability in Southern Lebanon ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 14 August 2025. Washington has sidelined the monitoring mechanism attached to the November 2024 ceasefire, in which UNIFIL and France (the Council’s penholder on Lebanon) were represented. Instead, an annex of the June framework agreement provides for a U.S.-headed “military coordination group”, through which Israel and Lebanon will manage tasks that UNIFIL or a successor force might have helped tackle, including “deconfliction, verification and overall implementation”. 58 The parties did not officially release this annex to the framework agreement, but they have not challenged the authenticity of a text leaked to the media in late June. “ The Lebanon-Israel ‘security’ annex agreement revealed ”, L’Orient Today , 29 June 2026. Other Council members and Lebanon strongly favour retaining an international presence, having reluctantly agreed to UNIFIL’s termination at the end of 2026 to avoid a U.S. veto that would have abruptly ended the mission in August 2025. 59 “ UN Interim Force in Lebanon: Vote on Final Mandate Renewal and Drawdown* ”, Security Council Report, 28 August 2025; Jamie Prentis, “ Lebanese MPs urge UN to extend peacekeeping mission ”, The National , 24 July 2026. The framework agreement does not mention the UN or Security Council resolution 1701. The annex, however, proposes a future role for a “mutually agreed-upon third-party entity” to verify that non-state armed groups have been cleared from each “pilot zone”. 60 “ The Lebanon-Israel ‘security’ annex agreement revealed ”, op. cit. To date, Israeli, Lebanese and U.S. negotiators have struggled to flesh out what such verification would entail, making it difficult for interested nations to commit troops to a mission that might prove dangerous. Yet even if the framework agreement eventually falls by the wayside, any other attempt to reach a deal that would link Israel’s withdrawal from southern Lebanon and cessation of airstrikes with an end to Hizbollah attacks on Israel and disarmament of the group would in all likelihood hinge on some sort of third-party verification. International partners have begun debating options for a new multinational presence. In June, the Secretary-General proposed a follow-up UN mission involving both armed and unarmed troops. 61 The report, mandated by the Security Council in Resolution 2790, proposed three different deployment sizes: the largest option would entail 5,525 uniformed personnel, the middle one 3,370 and the lightest footprint approximately 1,980. See “ Letter dated 1 June 2026 from the Secretary-General addressed to the President of the Security Council ”, UNSC S/2026/453, 1 June 2026. France and Italy have also announced plans to create a new multinational coalition in southern Lebanon as a successor to UNIFIL. 62 “ Lebanon president welcomes French, Italian efforts to form coalition to succeed UNIFIL ”, Arab News , 26 June 2026. In parallel, the European Union is weighing a separate mission comprising civilian and military personnel to advise and possibly train Lebanese forces – outside southern Lebanon – in addition to the €180 million it has already committed to support the Lebanese army. 63 Louay Faour, “ European powers seek greater role in south Lebanon’s post-war security architecture ”, The New Arab , 12 July 2026; Lili Bayer, “ EU diplomatic service proposes mission to train Lebanese forces, documents show ”, Reuters, 24 June 2026;“ European Peace Facility: Council adopts EUR 100 million assistance measure in support of the Lebanese Armed Forces ”, press release, Council of the EU, 4 June 2026. Any new multinational mission would have no choice but to work alongside the Lebanese-Israeli-U.S. security arrangement, even if that is not fully defined. States wishing to participate in a mission would almost certainly demand Security Council authorisation prior to sending troops to southern Lebanon so as to guarantee their legal and political protection. Given U.S. veto power, Washington’s support on the Council remains indispensable, meaning that UN members cannot circumvent the trilateral mechanism championed by the Trump administration. Between now and the end of December, diplomats should monitor the evolution of security arrangements on the ground in southern Lebanon, while seeking to work out with Washington what kind of international deployment, if any, would be beneficial to Lebanon and its stability. It is unlikely that any security arrangement, whether the June framework agreement and/or some future deal, will either fully disarm Hizbollah or completely dissuade Israel from conducting military operations in Lebanon. But withdrawing UNIFIL, with no immediate successor in place, could leave a vacuum that makes an already tense situation even more volatile. By inheriting UNIFIL’s most valuable functions – in particular, monitoring and on-the-ground deconfliction – a new multinational mission could set up a guardrail against fresh escalation. Ideally, that force would eventually assume other roles in bolstering a sustainable security arrangement for southern Lebanon that becomes durable enough to stand on its own feet. 2. Adapting the UN’s political strategy for Sudan The UN continues to be on the margins of diplomacy aimed at halting Sudan’s devastating civil war. Secretary-General Guterres’ appointment of Pekka Haavisto as the new UN envoy in February has offered the organisation an opportunity to refresh its approach. Ramtane Lamamra – the UN’s previous diplomatic lead – struggled to find a bridge between the main warring parties, the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), or to coordinate the array of mediators working to resolve the conflict. The UN has had varying degrees of success in securing local deals over aid access, and it continues to prepare for a possible role in overseeing aspects of a mooted ceasefire. 64 See the Sudan entry in Crisis Group Briefing, Ten Challenges for the UN in 2025-2026 , op. cit. It is hard to see the UN leading efforts to stop the war, given the number of powerful foreign states backing the belligerents, but it should use the coming months to support other diplomatic tracks and raise global awareness of the urgent need to end the fighting. 65 “ Sudan: Closed Consultations ”, Security Council Report, 17 April 2026. Nearly eighteen months ago, UN officials acknowledged that Sudan’s plight had become the world’s largest humanitarian catastrophe. 66 “ UN Sudan Annual Results Report 2024 ”, UN Sudan, 4 June 2025. Conditions have only deteriorated since then. An independent UN panel determined that mass killings, rapes and other atrocities committed by the RSF in October 2025 in El Fasher, Darfur – the city that hosted the headquarters of the former UN peacekeeping operation UNAMID – were “indicators of a genocidal path”. 67 “ Sudan: Hallmarks of Genocide in El Fasher - Report of the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan ”, UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), UN Doc A/HRC/61/77, 19 February 2026. Diplomats and UN officials alike are sounding the alarm about similar risks in El-Obeid, North Kordofan. 68 “ Sudan: Imminent offensive on El Obeid must be halted – Türk warns of catastrophic impact on civilians ”, press release, UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, 18 June 2026; “ Joint Statement of G7 Foreign Ministers on El Obeid, Sudan ”, U.S. Department of State, July 2026; “ Security Council Press Statement on Sudan (SC/16392) ”, UN Security Council, 20 June 2026. The two warring sides and their outside backers still believe there is more to gain from fighting than from negotiations. As matters stand, the country is in effect partitioned between the army and the RSF. 69 Crisis Group Africa Report N°211, Divided Sudan, Elusive Peace , 13 April 2026. To date, political negotiations have yielded few results. Much of the diplomatic focus has fallen on the Quad, a platform involving the U.S. and the three Arab powers with the most sway over the conflict parties – Egypt, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Its September 2025 roadmap, however, has won over neither belligerent, while Riyadh and Abu Dhabi, at loggerheads in conflict settings from Libya to Yemen, are doubling down on backing the army and RSF, respectively, stymying agreement within the Quad about what to do. 70 “ Joint Statement on Restoring Peace and Security in Sudan ”, U.S. Department of State, 12 September 2025; Comfort Ero and Alan Boswell, “ Latest Sudan Conference Shows Diplomacy is Backsliding ”, Crisis Group Analyst’s Notebook, 17 April 2026. In parallel, the UN is working alongside the African Union (AU), the EU, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), a Horn of Africa body, and the Arab League to support Sudanese-led civilian political dialogues as part of a nascent diplomatic track called the Quintet; these mediators convened a meeting in Berlin in April and another in Addis Ababa two months later. 71 “ Sudan: Quintet Joint Statement on de-escalation of the conflict in Sudan ”, European External Action Service, 11 February 2026; “ Quintet Statement on Ongoing Consultations with Sudanese Political Actors ”, African Union, 6 June 2026. Sudanese participants cannot agree on how to move forward with the talks, however. Having completed an initial tour of Sudan and the region, Haavisto can begin revising the UN’s diplomatic strategy. 72 “ Pekka Haavisto (Personal Envoy of the Secretary-General for Sudan) on the situation in the country – Press Conference ”, Office of the UN Spokesperson, 25 June 2026. He will need to reassure all parties that the UN will be an independent, impartial counterpart, even though the army-led government is the legally recognised one in New York. Haavisto needs to build rapport with others across Sudan’s fragmented political spectrum, including armed, political and civil players that are enlisted in the war, on one side or the other, or are non-aligned, as well as the various African, Arab and other countries directly involved in the conflict in one way or another. He will also need to reach out to the RSF, even if its deeds have earned it widespread and deserved condemnation. Lamamra struggled to maintain this balance, with critics seeing him as weighting his engagements too heavily toward the army-led authorities and its allies. 73 Crisis Group interviews, opposition political figures; RSF officials and allies, October-November 2025. Haavisto now has a chance for a reset. Haavisto should also strengthen the UN’s contributions within the Quintet. He could begin by stepping up outreach to various civilian groups between official Quintet meetings, with a view to mending fences between them. He could also help institute more consistent interactions between the Quintet and the army-led government, which has so far proven reluctant to get involved with a political process that is independent of its authority and takes place outside the country. 74 “ Quintet Statement Ahead of Visit to Khartoum, the Republic of Sudan, 8-10 September ”, Delegation of the European Union to the African Union, 8 September 2026. The army is instead pursuing its own “national dialogue” inside Sudan, which few of its political or armed opponents look likely to join. Behind the scenes, the UN should ... search for opportunities to bolster and connect the two diplomatic coalitions driving peace efforts [in Sudan]. Behind the scenes, the UN should also search for opportunities to bolster and connect the two diplomatic coalitions driving peace efforts, neither of which appears to have momentum at present. One way forward would be for Haavisto to work closely with counterparts to quietly float proposals for how Sudan could be governed whenever the main belligerents and their outside patrons summon the political will to seek an end to the war. Haavisto could help communicate these proposals to Quad and Quintet members, the two warring parties, and Sudan’s other main political movements and figures. Though it is hard to imagine a breakthrough any time soon given the entrenched positions on both sides, the UN should separately continue planning for a possible role in backing humanitarian access and ceasefire arrangements between the army and RSF should regional support for peace efforts eventually rise. 75 The UN is not formal member of the Quad, but it has worked informally with the U.S. to scope out technicalities of a monitoring mechanism for the prospective humanitarian truce that was outlined in the Quad’s September 2025 roadmap. The UN’s new leader should ensure that Haavisto and other UN envoys covering the Horn, central Africa and the Middle East remain in close contact in the hope of identifying opportunities to break the diplomatic deadlock among states in these areas. 3. Encouraging a role for the General Assembly in Gaza’s ceasefire Having repeatedly called for a ceasefire to halt Israel’s campaign against Hamas in Gaza from 2023-2025, the General Assembly has devoted little energy to discussing whether the mechanisms created to uphold it are working. The Security Council’s November 2025 endorsement of the Trump administration’s ceasefire plan in Resolution 2803 – including its highly unusual authorisation of a Trump-chaired Board of Peace to serve as Gaza’s transitional administration – has erected a de-facto firewall between the UN and the diplomatic apparatus overseeing the Palestinian enclave’s future, at least until the Board’s UN mandate expires at the end of 2027. 77 “Resolution 2803”, op. cit. With Gaza’s reconstruction at a virtual standstill and Israel tightening its grip on the territory, UN member states risk sitting idle as the U.S.-dominated Board veers further off course. 78 Crisis Group Middle East Report N°257, Hollow Promises: Resetting Gaza’s Ceasefire , 24 August 2026. The Board’s backtracking on the terms of its own fifteen-point roadmap – which features a scheme for decommissioning Hamas’s weapons agreed to by Palestinian factions but opposed by Israel – is just one of many troubling developments. The Security Council is, unfortunately, unlikely to consider corrective action until the Board mandate’s 2027 sunset. In the interim, member states should at a minimum use the General Assembly to assess the Board’s performance and to catalyse diplomatic pressure for putting Gaza on track toward recovery and Palestinian statehood. The General Assembly was the hub of UN diplomatic activity on Gaza throughout the war, as both President Joe Biden and President Trump blocked the Security Council from taking meaningful action. UN members convened the Assembly’s Emergency Special Session on the Occupied Palestinian Territories (its dedicated format for discussing the broader conflict) on eight separate occasions, and they debated five failed Security Council resolutions. 79 The General Assembly debated the nine vetoed resolutions under a Liechtenstein-led veto initiative, established by the General Assembly in April 2022. For full list of General Assembly meetings convened under the veto initiative, see “ Living with the Veto ”, Security Council Report, 23 March 2026, p. 8. Member states adopted five major General Assembly decisions on various aspects of the conflict, including the New York Declaration of September 2025, which bolstered recognition of Palestinian statehood. 80 “ Admission of new Members to the United Nations ”, UNGA A/RES/ES-10/23, 10 May 2024; Advisory Opinion of the International Court of Justice ”, UNGA A/RES/ES-10/24, 19 September 2024; “ Support for the mandate of the UN Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East ”, UNGA A/RES/ES-10/25, 16 December 2024; “ Protection of civilians and upholding legal and humanitarian obligations ”, UNGA A/RES/ES-10/27, 13 June 2025; “ Endorsement of the New York Declaration on the Peaceful Settlement of the Question of Palestine and the Implementation of the Two-State Solution ”, UNGA A/80/L.1/Rev.1, 10 September 2025. Though these measures had limited impact on the ground, they signalled growing international opposition to the war’s trajectory. The Security Council’s endorsement of Trump’s ceasefire plan upended these dynamics. By agreeing to the U.S.-drafted resolution (unenthusiastically supported by regional mediators and the State of Palestine), they in effect outsourced all responsibility for Gaza’s recovery and governance to the Board of Peace. 81 In Resolution 2803, the Security Council authorises the Board of Peace to set up a transitional administration (supervising a Palestinian technocratic committee, as well as matters including reconstruction of Gaza, public services, humanitarian assistance, movement of persons in and out of the strip and the envisioned International Stabilisation Force. “Resolution 2803”, op. cit.; Forti, Gowan and Rodenbeck, “What to Look for as the Gaza Peace Plan Comes to the UN Security Council”, op. cit. Since then, the UN has been further isolated from diplomacy on Gaza. It neither participates in any of the Board’s structures nor has it been asked to help stand up the International Stabilisation Force envisaged by the Council-approved Trump plan. 82 Sigrid Kaag, who was the former UN Gaza Humanitarian Coordinator and the former UN Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, is a member of the Board of Peace’s Gaza Executive Board. The Board’s High Representative Nickolay Mladenov (a former UN Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process) has briefed the Council and submitted a report (as required by Resolution 2803), but the General Assembly has discussed the situation only once – indirectly – since November 2025. No member state has asked to reconvene the Emergency Special Session despite worsening conditions under the tenuous truce. 83 General Assembly Annual Event of the Committee on the Exercise of the Inalienable Rights of the Palestinian People Commemorating the Nakba, 15 May 2026. The inattention seems particularly negligent given that Gaza’s circumstances are diverging from not only Resolution 2803, but also the array of General Assembly resolutions and international legal orders about Palestine. 84 Crisis Group Report, Hollow Promises: Resetting Gaza’s Ceasefire , op. cit. The lack of tangible progress in nearly a year after reaching a purported ceasefire makes international actors complicit in a brutal status quo: Gaza’s people are in effect hostage to diplomatic forces outside their control. Unless something changes, they will remain under siege, subject to bombardment and denied a future until the Board of Peace decides that Hamas has met Israel’s demands. Washington would likely veto any Security Council action perceived to criticise Israel – which receives unconditional backing from the U.S. at the UN – or to cast doubt on the legitimacy and efficacy of Trump’s peace efforts. But that ought not to be a justification for inaction in the General Assembly or elsewhere. UN members should use the General Assembly to challenge the Board of Peace’s unhelpful domination of the diplomatic space. UN members should use the General Assembly to challenge the Board of Peace’s unhelpful domination of the diplomatic space. The next meeting of the Global Alliance for the Two-State Solution, scheduled for September, could kickstart that endeavour. Member states should also consider reconvening the General Assembly’s Tenth Emergency Special Session to continue these efforts beyond High-Level Week. In addition, members should use these forums to offer political backing to the Palestinian technocratic committee as a means of asserting Palestinian ownership of reconstruction. These platforms provide an opportunity to reaffirm the necessity of the UN-led aid distribution network in Gaza, which remains the most capable one in the strip. Members might also signal the costs they would impose on Israel (bilaterally or in regional blocs) if it continues to obstruct provisions of the ceasefire and prevent the Palestinian technocratic committee from working in Gaza. 85 For example, on 8 September the British foreign secretary announced a raft of measures against Israel responding to its construction of illegal settlements in the West Bank and obstruction of the Trump ceasefire plan for Gaza. See Ed Miliband, “ Foreign Secretary Oral Statement on Israel-Palestine ”, speech to UK Parliament, 8 September 2026. For background, see Crisis Group Report, Hollow Promises: Resetting Gaza’s Ceasefire , op. cit. States should also consider tasking the Secretariat with preparing a report to evaluate follow-through on the New York Declaration, adopted a year ago, by the beginning of the 82nd General Assembly session in September 2027. The Declaration commits its signatories to a range of measures to end the war in Gaza, to facilitate a credible pathway toward Palestinian self-determination and to support a sovereign Palestinian state living peacefully alongside Israel. 86 “ Endorsement of the New York Declaration on the Peaceful Settlement of the Question of Palestine and the Implementation of the Two-State Solution ”, op. cit. Such a report could be useful as the Council considers whether to renew the Board of Peace’s mandate, which it must do by 31 December 2027. While UN members cannot circumvent the deeply flawed ceasefire plan altogether, they can work through the world body to keep a global spotlight on Gaza. It is past time for the General Assembly to recover a sense of urgency for mobilising diplomatic pressure in support of the ceasefire and keeping space open for the Palestinians to pursue self-determination. 4. Reinforcing security and justice support to Haiti International efforts to help restore security in Haiti have reached a decisive phase. The Gang Suppression Force (GSF), a multilateral mission authorised by the Security Council in September 2025 and backed with UN logistical support, landed in Haiti in June. 87 “ Resolution 2793 ”, UNSC S/RES/2793, 30 September 2025. Expected to be at full strength by the end of the year, the force faces the daunting task of confronting armed gangs that have held much of the country hostage for years. 88 Crisis Group Report, Undoing Haiti’s Deadly Gang Alliance , op. cit.; “ Situation of human rights in Haiti ”, UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights A/HRC/61/74, 23 March 2026. International efforts to staff, fund and equip the GSF are essential to ending this painful chapter in Haiti’s history. But even if this force puts gangs on the back foot, it will only be the start of a far longer campaign to bring peace to the country. Haiti’s government and international partners should work closely with the UN to build exit ramps for individuals willing to abandon the gangs and reinforce new judicial bodies to investigate and prosecute gang crimes. The GSF’s close working relationship with the UN could help it avoid the problems that plagued its predecessor, the Kenyan-led Multinational Security Support mission. A new UN support office services the force’s logistics needs (ranging from supplying rations and fuel to covering its medical services and constructing bases) and channels monetary contributions its way. 89 “ Budgets for the periods from 1 October 2025 to 30 June 2026 and from 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027 for the United Nations Support Office in Haiti ”, UNGA A/80/630, 10 February 2026. Reasonably predictable funding from the UN’s assessed budget has enabled eight countries to pledge enough troops to surpass the initial target of 5,500 personnel, though as of publication only around 1,200 troops are on the ground. 90 As of publication, the GSF included personnel sent from Chad, El Salvador, Guatemala, Jamaica, Mongolia and Sri Lanka. A separate UN trust fund has nearly $226 million in voluntary donations, which have been promised to cover the wages of deployed personnel. 91 As of 30 June, the Trust Fund had $233 million in total pledges, with $184 million in cash receipts. The UN had spent approximately $67 million of the cash receipts leaving $117 million in hand. “ Contributions to the Trust Fund for the Multinational Security Support (MSS) mission for Haiti authorised under SCR 2699 (2023) and Gang Suppression Force (GSF) authorised under SCR 2793 ”, UN, 13 July 2026; “ United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti: Report of the Secretary-General ”, UNSC S/2026/574, 14 July 2026, p. 10. These officials are coordinating with senior staff in BINUH, the UN political office in Haiti tasked with engaging Haitian counterparts on governance and human rights, and in the force’s logistics support office. Preserving UN operations in the Central African Republic UN peacekeepers have been at the forefront of international efforts to protect civilians and back peace initiatives in the Central African Republic (CAR) since first being dispatched to the country in 2014. The U.S. and China, two of the Council’s permanent members, have suggested that the mission, known as MINUSCA, should now begin preparing to exit, citing the progress the country has made toward stability. (Their own interest is to lower the cost of UN peacekeeping.) Elections held in late December 2025 without a major disruption may bolster their case. 103 Charles Bouëssel, “ Central African Republic: Consolidating Security Gains after the Elections ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 27 January 2026. But when renewing MINUSCA’s mandate in November, diplomats should ensure that the mission retains sufficient capacity to protect civilians and deter armed groups in the country’s troubled east, since it is the only entity that can provide a buffer against worsening instability in that region. MINUSCA continues to fill gaps that the Central African authorities cannot plug. A guarantor of the 2019 peace agreement, the UN mission oversees local peace dialogues and disarmament programs across the country. 104 The Union for Peace in the Central African Republic, Return, Reclamation and Rehabilitation and the Patriotic Movement for the Central African Republic are the most prominent armed groups participating in these disarmament programs. In many areas outside the capital Bangui, local institutions depend on the mission to build and repair government offices, supply logistical assistance and offer physical protection. The threat of insurgency in CAR is much lower than it was a few years ago, but pockets of insecurity persist along the country’s eastern borders. 105 Bouëssel, “ Central African Republic: Consolidating Security Gains after the Elections ”, op. cit.
